# Stepper

> Show where a person is in a multi-step flow and what is done.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/stepper

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.StepperCheckoutDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="16">
        <arc:Stepper x:Name="Checkout"
                     CurrentIndex="1"
                     IsNavigable="True"
                     StepSelected="OnStepSelected">
            <arc:StepperStep Id="account" Label="Account" Description="Create your login" />
            <arc:StepperStep Id="shipping" Label="Shipping" Description="Where should we send it" />
            <arc:StepperStep Id="payment" Label="Payment" Description="Card or invoice" />
            <arc:StepperStep Id="review" Label="Review" Description="Check and confirm" />
        </arc:Stepper>
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="Back" Variant="Ghost" Click="OnBackClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Continue" Variant="Secondary" Click="OnContinueClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Finish all" Variant="Secondary" Click="OnFinishClick" />
        </WrapPanel>
        <TextBlock x:Name="Selected"
                   Text="Choose a completed step to go back."
                   TextWrapping="Wrap"
                   Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextSecondary}" />
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class StepperCheckoutDemo : UserControl
{
    public StepperCheckoutDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnStepSelected(object? sender, StepperStepSelectedEventArgs e)
    {
        Selected.Text = $"Returned to step {e.Index + 1}: {e.Step.Label}";
    }

    private void OnBackClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Checkout.CurrentIndex = Math.Max(0, Checkout.CurrentIndex - 1);
    }

    private void OnContinueClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Checkout.CurrentIndex = Math.Min(Checkout.Steps.Count, Checkout.CurrentIndex + 1);
    }

    private void OnFinishClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Checkout.CurrentIndex = Checkout.Steps.Count;
    }
}
```

## When to use

`Stepper` shows the position in a fixed sequence of steps and which steps are finished. It sits above the content of
a flow, such as a checkout or an onboarding wizard, and tells the person how far they have come and what is left.
It only indicates progress: the step content, the validation and the rules for moving on stay in your application.

- **Checkout in an e-commerce store**: account, shipping, payment and review. The person sees that shipping is done
  and payment is next, and can return to shipping to change the address without losing the rest of the order.
- **Workspace setup in a SaaS admin console**: create the workspace, invite the team, add billing and review. When the
  payment step fails, the error appears on that step, where the person has to act.
- **Identity verification in fintech onboarding**: document upload, a selfie check, the home address and a final
  review. The steps are strict, so a later step never shows as complete before the earlier ones are done.
- **Multi-step imports in an internal tool**: upload a CSV, map the columns, preview the rows and confirm. A vertical
  stepper with a description per step explains each stage in a side panel.
- **A runbook in an operations console**: acknowledge, mitigate, verify and close an incident. The stepper states where
  the on-call team is in a procedure that always runs in the same order.

## When not to use

- **A single percentage of finished work**, such as an upload or a nightly export: use `Progress`, which shows one value
  against a whole. A stepper with one step per percent would be unreadable.
- **Sections that people open in any order**, such as the tabs of an account settings page: use `Tabs`. A stepper
  implies an order, and only completed steps can be chosen from it.
- **A history of events**, such as the audit trail of an order or the replies on a ticket: use `Timeline`. A timeline
  lists what happened over time; a stepper shows where a fixed flow stands now.
- **Content that is still loading**, such as the fields of a step while its data arrives: show `Skeleton` in the step
  body. The stepper itself has no loading state.
- **Choosing one value from several options**: use `Select`, `RadioGroup` or `SegmentedControl`. A stepper does not
  collect a value; it only reports the position in a flow.

## Usage

Give `Stepper` its steps and the index of the step in progress. `CurrentIndex` is zero-based. An index equal to the
step count marks every step complete. Steps are either written inline, as in the example below, or bound from a
collection.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:Stepper CurrentIndex="1">
        <arc:Stepper.Steps>
            <arc:StepperStep Label="Account" Description="Create your login" />
            <arc:StepperStep Label="Shipping" Description="Where should we send it" />
            <arc:StepperStep Label="Payment" Description="Card or invoice" />
            <arc:StepperStep Label="Review" Description="Check and confirm" />
        </arc:Stepper.Steps>
    </arc:Stepper>
</UserControl>
```

`Stepper` derives from Avalonia's `TemplatedControl`, not from an items control. It owns the whole flow: it lays out
the steps as one panel, draws the connectors between them and animates the flow as a unit. Each step is drawn
as one internal item inside the panel, which is why the stepper can fill the connectors in order when progress jumps. Because it is not an
items control, it has no `ItemTemplate`; the step content is always the label and the description.

Two rules shape the whole control:

- `CurrentIndex` is the single source of truth. Steps before it are complete, the step at it is current and steps after
  it are upcoming. A value below zero is treated as zero, and a value above the step count as the step count.
- A step's `Error` overrides its status. A step with an error is shown as failed even when it is before or after the
  current index, so set `Error` only on the step the person must fix.

### Anatomy

1. **Marker** (one per step): a 28 px disc with a 1 px inner outline in the strong border color. It shows the step
   number while the step is upcoming or current, a drawn check when it is complete, and an alert mark when it has an
   error.
2. **Halo**: a ring that grows 4 px outside the disc around the current step, in the accent-subtle color. A failed step
   uses a halo in the danger color at 16% strength instead.
3. **Connector**: a 2 px line between two markers. The track is the border color; the part that is already reached
   fills with the accent color.
4. **Label** (`StepperStep.Label`): the step name, 14 px with medium weight and a 20 px line height. Completed steps show
   it in the secondary text color, the current step and an error in the foreground color, and upcoming steps in the
   muted text color.
5. **Description** (`StepperStep.Description`): 12 px copy with a 16.8 px line height, 2 px below the label, in the muted
   text color. An `Error` replaces it in the danger color.
6. **Caption** (compact only): the current step's label and detail, with 12 px of space above them. It shows only in a
   horizontal stepper that is in compact mode.

The sizes come from the stepper's design tokens. Horizontally, each step takes its own column, with 16 px before the
next column and 12 px between the marker and the label row. Vertically, the marker sits on the left with 12 px between
it and the text, each step has 20 px below it (24 px when compact), and the first label line is offset 4 px so it
centers on the marker.

### Bound steps

`ItemsSource` takes precedence over the inline `Steps`; inline steps are ignored while it is set. Bind a collection of
`StepperStep` objects. The stepper observes the collection and each step, so changing a `Label`, a `Description` or an
`Error` on a step updates the stepper without rebuilding it.

```xml
<arc:Stepper ItemsSource="{Binding Steps}"
             CurrentIndex="{Binding CurrentStep, Mode=TwoWay}" />
```

Give each step a stable `Id`. The `Id` is the key for the step's motion, so a step keeps its own state animation when
the collection is reordered or a step is added before it.

### Binding to a view model

In an MVVM application the view model owns the steps, the current index and the rules for moving on. The stepper shows
them. With CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, the view model below keeps the flow state and marks a failed payment on its step.

```csharp
public partial class CheckoutViewModel : ObservableObject
{
    private readonly IOrderService _orders;

    public CheckoutViewModel(IOrderService orders)
    {
        _orders = orders;
    }

    public ObservableCollection<StepperStep> Steps { get; } = new()
    {
        new StepperStep("Account", "Create your login") { Id = "account" },
        new StepperStep("Shipping", "Where should we send it") { Id = "shipping" },
        new StepperStep("Payment", "Card or invoice") { Id = "payment" },
        new StepperStep("Review", "Check and confirm") { Id = "review" }
    };

    [ObservableProperty]
    private int _currentStep = 1;

    [RelayCommand]
    private async Task PayAsync()
    {
        var result = await _orders.PayAsync(OrderId);
        Steps[2].Error = result.IsSuccess ? null : result.Error;
        if (result.IsSuccess)
        {
            CurrentStep = 3;
        }
    }

    [RelayCommand]
    private void Continue()
    {
        CurrentStep = Math.Min(Steps.Count, CurrentStep + 1);
    }
}
```

```xml
<StackPanel Spacing="20">
    <arc:Stepper ItemsSource="{Binding Steps}"
                 CurrentIndex="{Binding CurrentStep}"
                 IsNavigable="True" />
    <arc:Button Content="Continue" Command="{Binding ContinueCommand}" />
</StackPanel>
```

- `CurrentIndex` is two-way by default, so the view model sees the step a person returns to when they choose a completed
  step. Writing `Mode=TwoWay` explicitly, as above, documents the intent.
- The stepper does not block a move. `Continue` above only moves forward; the rules that decide whether the person may
  leave a step belong in the view model, which sets `CurrentIndex` only when they pass.
- Set `Error` on the step from the view model and clear it with `null` or an empty string. The stepper treats both as
  "no error".

### Errors and recovery

An error belongs on the step that the person can fix. The status changes at once, the marker becomes an alert, and the
error text replaces the description, so the cause is visible where the action is.

- Set `Error` when the server rejects the step (a declined card, a document that is too large) and keep the person on
  that step. The `CurrentIndex` does not change, so the flow stays where it is.
- Clear `Error` as soon as the value changes or the person retries. A stale error on a step that was fixed reads as a
  second failure.
- An error on a completed step (for example, a payment that was reversed after review) turns that step into an alert
  while the current index stays put. Consider moving the current index back to that step so the person sees the cause
  in context.

### Vertical with error

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.StepperVerticalWithErrorDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="16">
        <arc:Stepper x:Name="Setup"
                     CurrentIndex="2"
                     Orientation="Vertical"
                     Width="320"
                     HorizontalAlignment="Left">
            <arc:StepperStep Id="account" Label="Account" Description="Create your login" />
            <arc:StepperStep Id="shipping" Label="Shipping" Description="Where should we send it" />
            <arc:StepperStep Id="payment" Label="Payment" Description="Card or invoice" />
            <arc:StepperStep Id="review" Label="Review" Description="Check and confirm" />
        </arc:Stepper>
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="Toggle error" Variant="Danger" Click="OnToggleErrorClick" />
        </WrapPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class StepperVerticalWithErrorDemo : UserControl
{
    public StepperVerticalWithErrorDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnToggleErrorClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        var payment = Setup.Steps[2];
        payment.Error = payment.Error is null ? "Card declined. Try another card." : null;
    }
}
```

`Orientation` set to `Vertical` gives a timeline: markers on the left, labels and descriptions beside them, and the
connectors running down. Use it in a side panel, a drawer or a column of a split layout, where the steps are read top to
bottom. Give it a width, as in the example below, so the labels wrap instead of overflowing the column.

```xml
<arc:Stepper ItemsSource="{Binding Steps}"
             CurrentIndex="2"
             Orientation="Vertical"
             Width="320" />
```

### Compact and current details

A horizontal stepper narrower than 480 px switches to compact mode by itself. Set `IsCompact="True"` to ask for compact
mode at any width. `IsCompact="False"` does not turn the automatic rule off: a narrow horizontal stepper is still
compact, so give a full stepper at least 480 px.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.StepperCompactDemo">
    <arc:Stepper CurrentIndex="2" IsCompact="True">
        <arc:StepperStep Id="account" Label="Account" Description="Create your login" />
        <arc:StepperStep Id="shipping" Label="Shipping" Description="Where should we send it" />
        <arc:StepperStep Id="payment" Label="Payment" Description="Card or invoice" />
        <arc:StepperStep Id="review" Label="Review" Description="Check and confirm" />
    </arc:Stepper>
</UserControl>
```

In compact mode the markers stay, the labels hide, and the caption under the stepper names the current step with its
description. A vertical stepper is never compact by this rule, because it has room for its labels.

`Details` decides which descriptions show. `StepperDetails.All` (the default) shows every description. `Current` shows
the description of the current step only, which keeps a long flow short in a tight space. Errors always show, whatever
the setting.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.StepperCurrentDetailsDemo">
    <arc:Stepper CurrentIndex="1" Details="Current">
        <arc:StepperStep Id="account" Label="Account" Description="Create your login" />
        <arc:StepperStep Id="shipping" Label="Shipping" Description="Where should we send it" />
        <arc:StepperStep Id="payment" Label="Payment" Description="Card or invoice" />
        <arc:StepperStep Id="review" Label="Review" Description="Check and confirm" />
    </arc:Stepper>
</UserControl>
```

```xml
<arc:Stepper ItemsSource="{Binding Steps}"
             CurrentIndex="2"
             IsCompact="True" />
<arc:Stepper ItemsSource="{Binding Steps}"
             CurrentIndex="1"
             Details="Current" />
```

### Navigable steps

Set `IsNavigable` to let people return to completed steps, by click or by keyboard. A read-only stepper, the default,
shows progress only: its items take no focus and ignore clicks. Handle `StepSelected` when the step has to do work
before the flow moves back, such as saving the draft of the current step.

```xml
<arc:Stepper ItemsSource="{Binding Steps}"
             CurrentIndex="{Binding CurrentStep, Mode=TwoWay}"
             IsNavigable="True" />
```

```csharp
stepper.StepSelected += (_, e) =>
{
    // e.Index is the completed step that was chosen; e.Step is its StepperStep.
    SaveDraft();
};
```

`StepSelected` is a routed event. Its arguments carry `Index`, the zero-based index of the chosen step, and `Step`, the
`StepperStep` itself. If no handler marks the event as handled, the chosen step becomes the current step. A handler that
sets `e.Handled = true` takes over: the index does not change, so the view model must set `CurrentIndex` itself when
the move should happen.

Code can choose a step the same way a click does with `Select(int index)`. It has no effect when `IsNavigable` is off,
when the index is out of range, or when the index is not before the current step.

Only completed steps can be chosen. The current step and the upcoming steps are not clickable, and a pointer press on a
completed step shrinks its marker slightly until the press ends; the step is chosen only when the pointer is released
over it.

### Example: billing setup for a new workspace

A SaaS admin console walks an owner through four steps: name the workspace, invite the team, add billing and review.
The billing step has failed because the card was declined. The stepper stays on that step, the marker is an alert and
the error text replaces the description, so the person sees what to fix and where. The footer offers a Back action,
which is a secondary button, and a single primary action, so the next step is obvious. Both the card and the footer sit
inside a panel with the standard surface and border, so the flow reads as one object on the page.

![A workspace setup card with a failed billing step and the next action](https://docs.tkcode.si/shots/Docs/Progress/Stepper/images/SetupWorkspace.webp)

```xml
<Border Width="680"
        Padding="24"
        CornerRadius="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource RadiusPanel}"
        Background="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Surface}"
        BorderBrush="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Border}"
        BorderThickness="1">
    <StackPanel Spacing="24">
        <TextBlock Text="Set up Acme Analytics"
                   FontSize="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TypeLG}"
                   FontWeight="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource WeightMedium}"
                   Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Foreground}" />
        <arc:Stepper CurrentIndex="2" Label="Workspace setup" CompleteLabel="Setup complete">
            <arc:Stepper.Steps>
                <arc:StepperStep Id="workspace" Label="Workspace" Description="Acme Analytics" />
                <arc:StepperStep Id="team" Label="Team" Description="Invite 6 people" />
                <arc:StepperStep Id="billing"
                                 Label="Billing"
                                 Description="Card or invoice"
                                 Error="Card declined. Try another card." />
                <arc:StepperStep Id="review" Label="Review" Description="Check and confirm" />
            </arc:Stepper.Steps>
        </arc:Stepper>
        <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="8" HorizontalAlignment="Right">
            <arc:Button Content="Back" Variant="Secondary" />
            <arc:Button Content="Continue" />
        </StackPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</Border>
```

The example uses inline steps because the content is fixed. For a flow that changes at run time, bind `ItemsSource`
as shown earlier. The failed step keeps its place in the sequence: the stepper never skips a step, and the view model
decides whether the person may leave the failed step.

### Content guidelines

- **Step label**: one or two words in sentence case that name the step: "Shipping", "Billing", "Review". Avoid verbs
  and full sentences; the description carries the detail.
- **Description**: a short hint about what happens in the step: "Card or invoice", "Invite 6 people". It is shown
  under the label and is what people read when the label is not enough.
- **Error**: say what is wrong and what to do, in the same terms as the step name. The error replaces the description,
  so it must stand alone.
- **Complete label**: a short statement that the flow is finished, such as "Setup complete" or "All steps complete".
  It is announced to assistive technology and shown in the compact caption.
- **Stepper label**: the name of the whole flow, such as "Checkout progress". It is the accessible name of the group.

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| Step 1 | Account |
| Please enter your shipping address here | Shipping |
| Error! | Card declined. Try another card. |
| Done | All steps complete |
| Proceed to the next step | Continue |
| Progress | Checkout progress |

### Best practices

**Do**

- Keep one stepper per flow and make the steps the same kind of thing: a stepper of pages, not a mix of pages and
  actions.
- Put the error on the step the person must fix and keep the current index on that step, so the cause and the action
  are in one place.
- Use `IsNavigable` only when returning to a completed step is safe. Save the draft of the current step first, in the
  view model or in `StepSelected`.
- Give every step a stable `Id` when the steps come from data, so each step keeps its own motion across changes.
- Set `Width` on a vertical stepper so the labels wrap inside the column.

**Avoid**

- Using the stepper for a flow people can enter at any point. Its order is fixed by `CurrentIndex`, and a jump to an
  upcoming step is not possible; use `Tabs` for free navigation.
- Setting `CurrentIndex` past the end to mean "done" in a flow that has an unfinished step. The index equal to the
  count marks every step complete, so the flow must really be finished.
- Putting long text into `Label`. A long label wraps in the step head and pushes the other steps out of alignment;
  move the detail into `Description`.
- Setting `Error` on many steps at once. Several alerts in a row make it unclear which step to fix first; mark the first
  failing step and explain the rest on the page.
- Relying on color alone for state. Each state has its own marker: a number, a check and an alert mark, so the flow
  reads without color.

### Common questions

**Does the stepper stop a person from moving forward when a step is invalid?** No. The stepper only displays
`CurrentIndex` and `Error`. Check the rules in your view model before you increase the index, and set `Error` on the
step that failed.

**Why can I not Tab to the current step?** With `IsNavigable` on, Tab stops on each completed step. The current step is
reached with the arrow keys from a completed step, and `End` moves to it. This keeps the Tab order short in long flows.

**How do I show only the title of the current step on a narrow screen?** Set `IsCompact="True"` on a horizontal
stepper. The markers stay and the caption below names the current step and its description. Without `IsCompact`, a
horizontal stepper narrower than 480 px does this on its own.

**How do I change the default names for assistive technology?** Set `Label` (default "Progress") for the flow and
`CompleteLabel` (default "All steps complete") for the end state. Each step name is generated from its label and its
state, such as "Account, Completed".

**What happens when the step count changes while the flow is running?** The stepper rebuilds its steps when the
collection changes and displays the index clamped to the new count; it does not rewrite `CurrentIndex`. Keep the index
in the view model in step with the collection so the person does not land on a different step after a change.

## API reference

### Stepper

Shows where someone is in a strict multi-step flow and which steps are done (Arc Stepper). Drive it with `CurrentIndex` (the step count marks the whole flow complete). When progress jumps across several steps the connectors fill one after another (80ms apart) from the previous current step, then the halo grows around the new current step; numbers turn into drawn checks or alerts. With `IsNavigable` completed steps can be chosen by click or keyboard (arrows between reachable steps, Home / End, Enter / Space). Horizontal steppers narrower than 30rem fold into markers with the current step named underneath. Steps come from `ItemsSource` or the inline `Steps`.

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ItemsSource` | `IEnumerable?` | `null` | Bound steps (`StepperStep` or any object, shown by its text); takes precedence over `Steps`. |
| `CurrentIndex` | `int` | `0` | Index of the step in progress; the step count marks every step complete. |
| `Orientation` | `Orientation` | `Horizontal` | Horizontal (default) or vertical. |
| `IsNavigable` | `bool` | `false` | Lets people return to completed steps (Arc `onStepSelect`); otherwise the stepper is read-only. |
| `Details` | `StepperDetails` | `All` | Which descriptions show (Arc `details`). |
| `IsCompact` | `bool` | `false` | Markers only; labels stay available to assistive technology. |
| `Label` | `string` | `"Progress"` | Accessible name (Arc `label`, "Progress"). |
| `CompleteLabel` | `string` | `"All steps complete"` | Announced, and shown in the compact caption, once every step is complete. |
| `IsComplete` | `bool` | – | *Read-only.* True when every step is complete. |

| Event | Arguments | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `StepSelected` | `StepperStepSelectedEventArgs` | Raised when a completed step is chosen by click or keyboard. |

Pseudo-classes: `:vertical`, `:compact`, `:caption-error`

Derives from `TemplatedControl`: every member of `TemplatedControl` works as well.

### StepperStep

One step of a `Stepper` (Arc `steps[]` entry).

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Id` | `string?` | `null` | Stable key, so each step keeps its own motion when the list changes. |
| `Label` | `string?` | `null` | Step name, shown beside its marker. |
| `Description` | `string?` | `null` | A short hint under the label. |
| `Error` | `string?` | `null` | Marks the step as failed: the marker becomes an alert and this message replaces the description. |

Derives from `AvaloniaObject`: every member of `AvaloniaObject` works as well.

Event arguments of `StepSelected`:

| Member | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Index` | `int` | The zero-based index of the completed step that was chosen |
| `Step` | `StepperStep` | The step that was chosen |

## Accessibility

- `Label` names the stepper, and it defaults to "Progress". Set it to the name of the flow, such as "Checkout progress".
- Each step is named with its state: "Account, Completed", "Review, Not started" or "Error", so a failed step is
  identified by name as well as by its alert mark.
- The current step is marked as the current step, and the stepper reports its position: "Step 3 of 4: Payment".
- Changes of step are announced politely, so the new position is read without moving focus. When every step is
  complete, `CompleteLabel` is announced instead.
- A read-only stepper takes no focus. It is read as a group with its steps and their states.
- A navigable stepper keeps focus on the steps. Focus is drawn as a ring 4 px outside the step head.
- Steps that are not reached yet are not focusable and are skipped by Tab.

### Keyboard

Keys apply when `IsNavigable` is on. Otherwise the stepper takes no focus.

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | Move between the completed steps; the current and upcoming steps are not Tab stops |
| `Right` / `Down`, `Left` / `Up` | Move to the next or previous reachable step (completed or current); in a right-to-left horizontal stepper, `Left` and `Right` swap |
| `Home` | Move to the first reachable step |
| `End` | Move to the last reachable step, normally the current step |
| `Enter` / `Space` | Choose the focused completed step, as a click does; they do nothing on the current or upcoming steps |

## Motion

- When progress jumps over several steps, the connectors fill one after another, and the new current marker gets a halo
  that grows in.
- A number turns into a drawn check when a step completes, or into an alert mark when it fails.
- A changed description rises in from a soft blur, and the space it occupies springs to its new height.
- Reduced motion applies every change at once.

| Change | Full | Reduced | Off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Progress moves forward or back | Connectors fill or drain one after another, 80 ms apart; the halo grows around the new current step | Immediate | Immediate |
| A step completes | The number pops in from 0.5 with a subtle blur and its check stroke is drawn | Immediate | Immediate |
| A step fails | The marker becomes an alert and the error text replaces the description | Immediate | Immediate |
| A description changes | The text rises in from a soft blur and the row springs to its new height | Immediate | Immediate |
| Marker and label colors | The marker colors cross over 240 ms; label colors change with a standard tween | Immediate | Immediate |

A press on a completed step shrinks its marker to 0.92. Pointer hover on a completed step brightens its label to the
foreground color.

## Related

- `Progress` when the work has a percentage rather than steps.
- `Tabs` when the person can switch between sections in any order.
- `Skeleton` when the content of a step is still loading.

| Component | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `Progress` | One value shows how much of a single task is finished |
| `Tabs` | Sections are peers and can be opened in any order |
| `Timeline` | A list of events over time is the content, such as an order history |
| `Skeleton` | The content of a step is loading and has no shape yet |
| `Breadcrumb` | The person needs to see the path to a page, not the progress through a flow |
| `Select` / `RadioGroup` | The step asks for one value from a list of options |

# Countdown

> A launch countdown with rolling digits that morphs into a live state at zero.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/countdown

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.CountdownLaunchDemo">
    <arc:Countdown x:Name="Launch" />
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class CountdownLaunchDemo : UserControl
{
    public CountdownLaunchDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        Launch.Target = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow + new TimeSpan(3, 7, 42, 18);
    }
}
```

## When to use

`Countdown` shows the time left until a fixed moment, or through a fixed length of time, as rolling digits. Use it where
the remaining time is the main message of a page or a row. When the moment arrives, the control changes to its live
state by itself, so the screen does not need a timer of its own to switch the wording.

- **Launch and event pages**: a product launch, a conference keynote or a webinar that starts at a fixed time. The
  large variant gives the page a focal point above the fold, and the digits make the start time easy to read at a
  glance.
- **Sale and promotion windows**: a flash sale in a checkout banner or on a pricing page, with `Target` set to the
  closing moment. The control switches to "Live now" when the offer opens, without a server round trip for the change.
- **Deadlines in tables and cards**: a payment due date in a billing list, an invoice that expires or a trial that ends
  in a subscription row. The `Compact` variant is a single pill that fits a table cell at a fixed height.
- **Holds and access windows**: a seat reservation in a ticketing flow, or an early-access window in a developer
  console. `Duration` counts down a fixed length from when the control is shown, and `IsPaused` freezes it while the
  visitor waits on another step.
- **Scheduled maintenance on a status page**: the time left in a maintenance window, with `CompleteContent` set to
  "Maintenance in progress" so the state that follows the countdown is stated in the same place.

## When not to use

- **A site banner with a countdown and an action button**: use `AnnouncementBar`, which carries the message, the action
  and the dismiss control in one strip.
- **Progress through known work**: use `Progress` for a share of finished work. A countdown shows time left, not
  how much of a job is done.
- **Consumption against a fixed limit**: use `UsageMeter` for storage, seats or API calls measured against a quota.
- **Alerts that must reach a screen reader as the deadline nears**: `Countdown` is not a live region and does not
  announce its changes. Raise an `Alert` or a `Toast` at the moment that needs attention.
- **A number that moves with data**: use `AnimatedCounter` for a total that changes as data arrives, such as orders
  received today. A countdown runs on the clock and only moves toward zero.

## Usage

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:Countdown Label="Launch in" />
</UserControl>
```

Set `Target` to the moment to count down to, or `Duration` to count down a fixed length from when the control is shown.
The default is the large variant with days, hours, minutes and seconds.

```csharp
launch.Target = new DateTimeOffset(2030, 1, 1, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
```

`Countdown` derives from Avalonia's `TemplatedControl`, so the usual surface properties (`Background`, `BorderBrush`,
`BorderThickness`, `CornerRadius` and `Padding`) are forwarded to its shell, and `Foreground`, `FontFamily` and
`FontSize` are set by the theme. The theme sets the digit and unit typography from the Arc tokens, so a page can change
the colors and spacing without touching the template. The countdown does not take focus, and it has no visible label:
`Label` is the accessible name only.

### Anatomy

1. **Shell**: a border that springs to the size of the content it holds, so the width changes when a
   unit group appears or leaves. The large variant has no background or border of its own. The compact variant draws a
   1 px border in the border color on the surface color, with a pill radius and 12 px of horizontal padding.
2. **Digit wheels**: each digit is a clipped wheel that feathers at its top and bottom edges. In the large
   variant the digits use the display font at medium weight with display tracking, and their size follows the width of
   the control: 12.5% of the width, between 28 px and 72 px. In the compact variant the digits use the body font with no
   tracking and the size of the text.
3. **Unit names**: under each group in the large variant, in the muted text color at the extra-small type size. In the
   compact variant, a quiet unit letter follows each group at the small type size.
4. **Separators**: a colon between the groups in the large variant. The compact variant shows the groups in one line.
5. **Completion**: a 10 px success-colored pulse dot and the `CompleteContent` text. In the large
   variant the text uses the display font at medium weight and the size of 11% of the width, between 28 px and 52 px.
   In the compact variant the text uses the body font in the success color.

### Choosing a variant

Use `Large` (the default) when the countdown is the main content of its area: a hero block, an event header or a
dashboard card with room for four groups. The large digits need about 320 px of width to show four groups, so give it a
full column or a card rather than a sidebar cell.

Use `Compact` when the countdown is one fact among others: a banner, a table cell, a card footer or a sentence in a
notice. The pill is at least 32 px high and sizes to its text, so it keeps a table row at its usual height.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.CountdownCompactDemo">
    <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
        <arc:Countdown x:Name="Deadline" Variant="Compact" />
        <arc:Countdown x:Name="Hours" Units="Hours, Minutes" Variant="Compact" />
        <arc:Countdown x:Name="Keynote" Variant="Compact" Label="Keynote starts in" />
    </WrapPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class CountdownCompactDemo : UserControl
{
    public CountdownCompactDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        Deadline.Target = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow + new TimeSpan(0, 5, 12, 40);
        Hours.Target = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow + new TimeSpan(1, 2, 30, 0);
        // A wall-clock time in a named zone resolves to one fixed moment.
        Keynote.Target = Countdown.ResolveTarget("2030-01-01T09:00:00", TimeZoneInfo.Utc);
    }
}
```

```xml
<arc:Countdown Variant="Compact"
               Units="Hours, Minutes"
               Label="Offer ends in" />
```

### Choosing units

`Units` lists the units to show, largest first. The largest unit listed absorbs everything above it, so `Hours` alone
shows 51 hours for a window of two days and three hours. The default is days through seconds, which suits a launch that
is more than a day away. A window measured in hours reads better with `Hours, Minutes`, and a short hold reads best with
`Minutes, Seconds`.

| Value | Shows |
|---|---|
| `Days` | Whole days; the largest unit absorbs the hours and below |
| `Hours` | Whole hours; can exceed 24 when days are not shown |
| `Minutes` | Whole minutes |
| `Seconds` | Whole seconds |
| `All` | Days, hours, minutes and seconds (the default) |

The flags combine, for example `Hours | Minutes`. `None` is treated as `All`. Changing `Units` or `Variant` at run time
updates the groups in place, so a page can switch between a short and a long display without recreating the control.

```xml
<arc:Countdown Units="Minutes, Seconds"
               Duration="00:00:12" />
```

### Target and duration

Use `Target` for a deadline that is the same for every visitor: a launch, a sale close or an expiry date stored on
the server. Use `Duration` for a length of time that starts when the control is shown: a checkout hold, a trial
timer or a review window. When both are set, `Target` takes precedence.

A target countdown keeps counting to the same instant after the visitor leaves and returns. A duration countdown keeps
its remaining time while it is off screen, so a visitor who switches away and back sees the time that was left.

### Time zones and the clock

Parse a target with `ResolveTarget` when the text has no offset. Target text with `Z` or an offset is exact.
Wall time is read in the time zone you pass, so every visitor counts down to the same moment.

```csharp
countdown.Target = Countdown.ResolveTarget("2030-01-01T09:00:00", timeZone);
```

`ResolveTarget` does not read the device's time zone. Wall time is resolved for the date it names, so daylight saving
applies to that date. A wall-clock time that does not exist on that date, because the clocks skipped it, resolves to the
later instant.

Pass a `TimeProvider` through the `TimeProvider` property when the device clock cannot be trusted. A server-synced
provider keeps the display and the completion moment on the same clock for every visitor. The default is
`TimeProvider.System`.

### Pause, resume and restart

A duration countdown keeps its remaining time while it is paused. A target countdown keeps counting to the same
moment, so pausing only freezes the display. `Completed` still fires on time when a target is paused.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.CountdownDurationWithPauseDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="16">
        <arc:Countdown x:Name="Timer"
                       Duration="0:0:12"
                       Units="Minutes, Seconds"
                       Completed="OnCompleted" />
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button x:Name="PauseButton"
                        Content="Pause"
                        Variant="Secondary"
                        Click="OnPauseClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Restart" Variant="Ghost" Click="OnRestartClick" />
        </WrapPanel>
        <TextBlock x:Name="Status"
                   Text="Counting down 12 seconds."
                   TextWrapping="Wrap"
                   Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextSecondary}" />
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class CountdownDurationWithPauseDemo : UserControl
{
    public CountdownDurationWithPauseDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnCompleted(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Status.Text = "Completed fired.";
    }

    private void OnPauseClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Timer.IsPaused = !Timer.IsPaused;
        PauseButton.Content = Timer.IsPaused ? "Resume" : "Pause";
    }

    private void OnRestartClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Timer.Restart();
        Timer.IsPaused = false;
        PauseButton.Content = "Pause";
        Status.Text = "Counting down 12 seconds.";
    }
}
```

```xml
<arc:Countdown Duration="00:00:12"
               IsPaused="{Binding IsTimerPaused, Mode=TwoWay}" />
```

```csharp
timer.Pause();
timer.Resume();
timer.Restart(); // starts a duration again from its full length
```

`IsPaused` is two-way, so a view model can read the state and a button can bind to it. `Restart` clears the completed
state and starts a duration from its full `Duration` again. For a target, `Restart` re-reads the target.

### Completion

`CompleteContent` replaces the digits at zero, beside a pulsing live dot. It defaults to "Live now". Handle
`Completed` to react once, at the moment the countdown reaches zero.

```csharp
timer.CompleteContent = "Registration is open";
timer.Completed += (_, _) => offers.Refresh();
```

`Completed` is raised only while the countdown is shown and reaches zero. A target that has already passed when the
control is shown displays the completed state at once and does not raise `Completed`, so a page that loads after a sale
closed does not run the offer code twice. `Remaining` is zero once the countdown is complete, and `IsCompleted` tells
the view model which state is on screen.

### Example: Product launch on an event page

A launch page needs one fact above the fold: when the product is available. The countdown is the hero of the block,
with the large variant, a short line of context and one action. The copy names the offer and its end, so the visitor
knows what the number means. The example uses a duration so that the scene is stable on every capture. A launch that every visitor should see
end at the same moment uses `Target` instead, with the moment written in UTC or with an offset.

![A launch hero with a large countdown, an early-access note and a primary action](https://docs.tkcode.si/shots/Docs/Progress/Countdown/images/LaunchHero.webp)

```xml
<Border Width="680"
        Padding="32"
        CornerRadius="12"
        Background="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Surface}"
        BorderBrush="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Border}"
        BorderThickness="1">
    <StackPanel Spacing="24">
        <StackPanel Spacing="6">
            <TextBlock Text="Northwind Commerce 2026 Summer Release"
                       FontSize="20"
                       FontWeight="SemiBold"
                       Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Foreground}" />
            <TextBlock Text="Early-access pricing ends when the countdown reaches zero."
                       FontSize="14"
                       TextWrapping="Wrap"
                       Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextMuted}" />
        </StackPanel>
        <arc:Countdown Duration="3.07:42:18" />
        <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="Reserve early access" Variant="Primary" />
            <arc:Button Content="View pricing" Variant="Ghost" />
        </StackPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</Border>
```

The layout gives the countdown the full width of the card, so the large digits scale to the largest size the theme
allows without crowding the copy. The primary action is one verb and an object. The secondary action is a ghost button,
so the page has one clear next step.

### Content guidelines

The countdown has no visible label, so the words next to it carry the meaning. Write the deadline in full beside the
digits, and write `CompleteContent` as a short state that reads correctly after the time has run out. Use sentence case,
numbers as digits, and no urgency words in the copy. The control keeps the digits and the unit names; the surrounding
text says what they count to.

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| `Hurry, the time is nearly up` | `Early-access pricing ends 2026-10-29 at 09:00 UTC` |
| `Time remaining` (as the only text) | `Registration closes in`, with the time zone in the line below |
| `Done` | `Live now` or `Registration is open` |
| `Countdown expired` | `Offer closed`, when the offer no longer applies |

Keep `CompleteContent` to two or three words so it fits the compact pill. Put the time zone in the text, never only in
the countdown, because the digits do not say which zone the moment belongs to.

### Best practices

**Do**

- Set `Target` with an offset or a time zone for a deadline that every visitor shares, because the same moment then
  reads the same on every device.
- Name the deadline in the text next to the countdown, because the digits alone do not say what happens at zero.
- Use `Compact` in table rows and banners, because the large digits make a dense list hard to scan.
- Pass a server-synced `TimeProvider` when the device clock cannot be trusted, such as a checkout that closes a hold.

**Avoid**

- Using a countdown for a deadline the person must act on in a few seconds, because the control is not announced as it
  changes. Raise an `Alert` or a `Toast` when the outcome matters.
- Several large countdowns on one screen, because each one moves every second and draws the eye away from the page.
- Reading the time zone from the device for a target, because a visitor in another zone then counts to a different
  moment. Use `ResolveTarget` with the zone the event belongs to.
- Restarting a target countdown to mean a new deadline. `Restart` re-reads the same target; set a new `Target` instead.

### Common questions

**What does the countdown show when the target has already passed?** It shows the completed state at once, with
`CompleteContent`, and it does not raise `Completed`. Check `IsCompleted` in your view model if the page should show a
different layout for a closed offer.

**How do I count down a fixed length, such as a 15-minute hold?** Set `Duration` to `00:15:00` and `Units` to
`Minutes, Seconds`. The countdown starts when it is shown. Bind `IsPaused` to a view model property so a checkout step
can hold the timer while the visitor reads a form.

**Why does the countdown not update while the window is hidden?** The clock stops ticking when the control is off screen
or not in the visual tree. A duration keeps its remaining time while it is away, and a target keeps counting to the same
instant, so the display is correct when it returns.

**How do I react when the countdown ends?** Handle the routed `Completed` event, or subscribe in code with
`timer.Completed += (_, _) => offers.Refresh();`. The event fires once, while the control is shown and reaches zero.

## API reference

### Countdown

Counts down to a fixed moment, or through a duration, with rolling digit wheels (Arc Countdown), and morphs into a live label at zero. The clock ticks just after each whole second, only while the countdown is on screen; a separate `PausableTimer` makes `Completed` land on time even while ticking is paused. A `Duration` countdown can be paused and resumed (`IsPaused`, `Pause`, `Resume`); a `Target` countdown counts to a fixed instant, so pausing only freezes the display. Wheels turn the short way round; the shell springs to the size of whatever it holds.

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Target` | `DateTimeOffset?` | `null` | The moment to count down to. Takes precedence over `Duration`. |
| `Duration` | `TimeSpan?` | `null` | Counts down this long from when the countdown is shown (or restarted); pausable. |
| `Units` | `CountdownUnits` | `All` | Units to show, largest first; the largest absorbs the rest. Defaults to days through seconds. |
| `Variant` | `CountdownVariant` | `Large` | Large display digits with unit names (default) or one compact pill. |
| `CompleteContent` | `object?` | `"Live now"` | Shown once the countdown reaches zero, beside a pulsing live dot (Arc `completeLabel`, "Live now"). |
| `Label` | `string` | `"Time remaining"` | Accessible name (Arc `label`, "Time remaining"). |
| `TimeProvider` | `TimeProvider` | – | Clock source; pass a server-synced provider when device time cannot be trusted. |
| `IsPaused` | `bool` | `false` | Pauses a duration countdown (remaining time is kept); freezes the display of a target countdown. |
| `Remaining` | `TimeSpan` | – | *Read-only.* Time left, read from the clock on every tick. |
| `IsCompleted` | `bool` | – | *Read-only.* True once the countdown has reached zero. |

| Event | Arguments | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Completed` | `RoutedEventArgs` | Raised once, the moment the countdown reaches zero while it is shown. |

Pseudo-classes: `:complete`, `:compact`

Derives from `TemplatedControl`: every member of `TemplatedControl` works as well.

### Companion types

`CountdownUnits` is a flags enum. The members are listed here because `Units` takes a combination of them.

| Member | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Days` | Days; absorbs hours and below when it is the largest unit shown |
| `Hours` | Hours; absorbs minutes and seconds when it is the largest unit shown |
| `Minutes` | Minutes |
| `Seconds` | Seconds |
| `All` | Days, hours, minutes and seconds |
| `None` | No units selected; treated as `All` |

`CountdownVariant` has two members: `Large` (display digits with unit names, the default) and `Compact` (one pill for
banners and table cells).

## Accessibility

- `Label` names the countdown. The default is "Time remaining".
- The control has no live region. Spoken text gives the time left without seconds when more than a minute remains,
  and reads `CompleteContent` once the countdown is over. A non-text `CompleteContent` is spoken as "Complete".
- The visible digits are not announced as they change, so a screen reader does not repeat every second.
- The control type is Text. The visible digits are in the raw view, and the spoken text is the value that assistive
  technology reads.
- Use a text line next to the countdown that names the deadline in full, for example "Closes 2026-10-29 at 09:00 UTC".
  A countdown alone does not say what it counts to.

### Keyboard

`Countdown` is not focusable and has no keyboard interaction. Put the controls that act on it, such as a Pause button
in the same group, in the tab order and bind them to `IsPaused`.

## Motion

- Each digit is a wheel that turns the short way round, with soft edges at the top and bottom of the window.
- The digits roll in one after another the first time they are shown. After that they change once per second.
- Units appear and disappear with the container springing to its new size.
- At zero the digits fade and scale into the completion label, and the live dot pulses.
- Reduced motion makes the wheels jump to the new value, sizes the container at once, switches content with a
  fade and stops the pulse.

| Change | Full | Reduced | Off |
|---|---|---|---|
| A digit changes each second | The wheel turns the short way; blur grows with the distance it travels | The digit jumps to the new value | Immediate |
| The first values appear | Digits roll in from zero, staggered 35 ms apart, up to 0.3 s | The digits show at once | Immediate |
| A unit group appears or leaves | Width springs with a morph, height with a smooth spring | The container takes its new size at once | Immediate |
| Reaching zero | Digits fade and scale to 0.92 into the completion label | The content switches with a fade | Immediate |
| The live dot | Pulses on a two-second cycle | Stops | Stops |

### Using motion with restraint

The digits move once a second, which is enough to show that the time is running. Keep the rest of the page still, and
do not stack a second moving element beside a countdown, such as a shimmering banner or a looping animation. Use one
countdown per screen region. Several countdowns in a long table each move every second, so keep a table to compact
pills and a few rows.

## Related

- `AnnouncementBar` for a site banner with a countdown and an action button.
- `Progress` when the work has a known amount of progress rather than a deadline.
- `UsageMeter` for consumption against a fixed quota, such as storage or seats.
- `Stepper` when the countdown is one part of a multi-step flow.
- `Alert` or `Toast` for a message that must be announced when a deadline passes.

| Component | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `AnnouncementBar` | A site-wide strip needs a countdown, a message and a button |
| `Progress` | The share of finished work is known |
| `UsageMeter` | A quota or limit is measured against current use |
| `Stepper` | The countdown belongs to one step of a flow |
| `Alert` / `Toast` | A deadline outcome must be announced to the visitor |
