# Activity heatmap

> See a year of activity at a glance, one square per day.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/activity-heatmap

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.ActivityHeatmapContributionsDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="12">
        <arc:ActivityHeatmap x:Name="Heatmap"
                             Label="Contributions in 2025"
                             Period="2025"
                             DateSelected="OnDateSelected">
            <arc:ActivityHeatmap.Actions>
                <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="4">
                    <arc:Button Content="2024" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small" Click="On2024Click" />
                    <arc:Button Content="2025" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small" Click="On2025Click" />
                </StackPanel>
            </arc:ActivityHeatmap.Actions>
        </arc:ActivityHeatmap>
        <TextBlock x:Name="Selected"
                   Text="Click a day or press Enter on it."
                   FontSize="13"
                   TextWrapping="Wrap"
                   Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextMuted}" />
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class ActivityHeatmapContributionsDemo : UserControl
{
    private readonly List<ActivityDay> _days2024 = Year(2024, 5);
    private readonly List<ActivityDay> _days2025 = Year(2025, 11);

    public ActivityHeatmapContributionsDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        Heatmap.ItemsSource = _days2025;
    }

    private void On2024Click(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) => Show(2024, _days2024);

    private void On2025Click(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) => Show(2025, _days2025);

    // Replace the days, the period and the label together; the grid recolors in a sweep.
    private void Show(int year, List<ActivityDay> days)
    {
        Heatmap.ItemsSource = days;
        Heatmap.Period = year.ToString();
        Heatmap.Label = $"Contributions in {year}";
    }

    private void OnDateSelected(object? sender, ActivityHeatmapDateSelectedEventArgs e)
        => Selected.Text = $"Selected {e.Date:MMM d, yyyy}: {e.Count} contributions (level {e.Level})";

    /// <summary>A year of activity with a weekday rhythm, streaks and quiet weeks (deterministic).</summary>
    private static List<ActivityDay> Year(int year, int seed)
    {
        var random = new Random(seed);
        var days = new List<ActivityDay>();
        var streak = 0;
        for (var date = new DateOnly(year, 1, 1); date.Year == year; date = date.AddDays(1))
        {
            if (streak <= 0 && random.NextDouble() < 0.08)
            {
                streak = random.Next(3, 12);
            }
            var weekend = date.DayOfWeek is DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday;
            var quiet = date.DayOfYear % 61 < 6;
            var busy = streak-- > 0;
            var count = quiet ? 0 : random.NextDouble() < (weekend ? 0.55 : 0.18) ? 0 : random.Next(1, busy ? 14 : 7);
            days.Add(new ActivityDay(date, count));
        }
        return days;
    }
}
```

## When to use

`ActivityHeatmap` shows how a count is spread across days, one square per day, with weeks as columns. It answers
questions about rhythm and continuity: is the team shipping every week, how long was the quiet spell in August, which
weekdays are busy. It fits a dashboard panel or a profile page where the whole period matters more than any one value.

- **Deploy and release frequency in a developer console**: a platform team reviews production deploys per day over the
  last quarter. Streaks and gaps are the story, and a day with no deploys reads as a gap rather than a missing value.
- **Engagement on a SaaS admin dashboard**: active users or completed onboarding steps per day for a workspace, shown
  next to the account's plan so the team sees whether usage grew through the year.
- **Workouts, study time or reading in a consumer app**: a profile page where each day is a square and the streak is
  visible at a glance. The legend explains the five levels without a separate chart.
- **Incident or support volume in an operations tool**: tickets opened per day across a quarter. A busy week stands
  out, and the selected day can open the list of tickets for that date.
- **Activity audit in an internal tool**: sign-ins or approvals per day for a compliance review, where the reviewer
  selects a day and reads its count before opening the detail view.

## When not to use

- **Exact comparison between days or periods**: use `BarChart`, where each bar has a length that can be compared
  precisely.
- **Choosing a date for input**: use `Calendar` for a date that a person picks for a booking, a due date or a report
  range. `ActivityHeatmap` selects a day for inspection, not for data entry.
- **A trend of a value over time**: use `LineChart` when the shape of a continuous value matters, such as revenue or
  latency, and the exact value at each point is important.
- **A compact trend beside a single number**: use `Sparkline`, which is small enough for a table row or a KPI card
  and shows the direction of a value rather than each day.
- **Periods shorter than a few weeks**: with only a handful of days the squares are too few to show a pattern, and a
  `BarChart` with labeled values is easier to read.
- **Several years side by side**: a grid that spans two years becomes twice as wide and scrolls sideways. Use one
  `ActivityHeatmap` per year, or a `BarChart` of yearly totals for the comparison.

## Usage

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:ActivityHeatmap Label="Contributions in 2025"
                         Period="2025"
                         ItemsSource="{Binding Days}" />
</UserControl>
```

`ActivityHeatmap` derives from Avalonia's `Control`, not from an items control. It draws the summary line, the month
and weekday labels, the day grid, the tooltip and the legend itself, so one control holds the whole calendar and no
item templates are needed. Because the grid is a single focusable control with arithmetic hit testing, it handles the
roughly 370 squares of a year without creating a visual per container.

### Anatomy

1. **Summary line**: the total count as an animated number, the unit noun, then "in" and the period. The total is
   set in the body size of 14 px and rolls to a new value when the data changes. `Period` hides the "in" and the
   period when it is empty.
2. **Actions** (`Actions`): any controls, placed at the right end of the summary line. When the summary and the actions
   do not fit side by side, the actions move to their own row under the summary.
3. **Weekday column**: a 30 px column of weekday labels on the left of the grid. It stays in place when a narrow grid
   scrolls sideways.
4. **Month labels**: abbreviated month names above the first week of each month, formatted with `Culture`. A partial
   first month loses its label when the next month starts fewer than three weeks later, so the labels never collide.
5. **Day grid**: one square per calendar day, with weeks as columns. Squares are 3 px apart. Their size follows the
   container width and stays between 9 px and 15 px. Days outside the data range are empty cells.
6. **Tooltip**: one bubble for the whole grid, showing the count and the date of the day under the pointer or the
   keyboard focus.
7. **Legend**: a caption that names the days at the highlighted level, then "Less", five swatches (levels 0 to 4)
   and "More". Hovering or focusing a swatch previews its level on the grid, and clicking it pins the level, which
   highlights the squares at that level. Click it again to clear the pin.

The header, the grid and the legend are separated by 16 px. The five tints are derived from the accent color: level 0
is the foreground mixed at 6.5% into the surface, and levels 1, 2 and 3 are the accent mixed at 26%, 50% and 76% into
that base. Level 4 is the full accent color.

### Years and controls

Replace `ItemsSource`, `Period` and `Label` together when the year changes, so the summary, the grid and the grid's
accessible name agree. `Actions` places controls beside the summary, such as a year switch. The grid recolors in a
sweep instead of redrawing, so a year switch keeps the page calm.

```xml
<arc:ActivityHeatmap Label="Contributions in 2025" Period="2025" ItemsSource="{Binding Days}">
    <arc:ActivityHeatmap.Actions>
        <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="4">
            <arc:Button Content="2024" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small" Command="{Binding ShowPrevious}" />
            <arc:Button Content="2025" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small" Command="{Binding ShowCurrent}" />
        </StackPanel>
    </arc:ActivityHeatmap.Actions>
</arc:ActivityHeatmap>
```

The grid always spans from the earliest to the latest date in the data. Pass one calendar year for a year view. If the
data holds two years, the grid becomes twice as wide and scrolls sideways, which is rarely what a reader wants, so
split the data by year.

### Units and weeks

`UnitOne` and `UnitOther` set the singular and plural noun for the count. The noun is singular only when the total is
exactly 1, so "1 workout" and "2 workouts" both read correctly. `FirstDayOfWeek` sets the first row of each week
column, which is Sunday by default; choose Monday for a work calendar. `Culture` formats dates and numbers, and its
default is en-US.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.ActivityHeatmapCustomUnitDemo">
    <arc:ActivityHeatmap x:Name="Heatmap"
                         Label="Workouts, last six months"
                         Period="the last six months"
                         UnitOne="workout"
                         UnitOther="workouts"
                         FirstDayOfWeek="Monday"
                         MaxWidth="520" />
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class ActivityHeatmapCustomUnitDemo : UserControl
{
    public ActivityHeatmapCustomUnitDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();

        // Six months of workouts, fewer on weekends (deterministic).
        var random = new Random(21);
        var days = new List<ActivityDay>();
        for (var date = new DateOnly(2025, 5, 1); date.Month <= 10; date = date.AddDays(1))
        {
            var weekend = date.DayOfWeek is DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday;
            var rest = random.NextDouble() < (weekend ? 0.6 : 0.25);
            days.Add(new ActivityDay(date, rest ? 0 : random.Next(1, 5)));
        }
        Heatmap.ItemsSource = days;

        // Fixed bounds for levels one to three; a count above the last bound is level four.
        Heatmap.Thresholds = [1, 2, 3];
    }
}
```

```xml
<arc:ActivityHeatmap Label="Workouts, last six months"
                     Period="the last six months"
                     UnitOne="workout"
                     UnitOther="workouts"
                     FirstDayOfWeek="Monday"
                     MaxWidth="520"
                     ItemsSource="{Binding Workouts}" />
```

`MaxWidth` keeps a six-month grid from stretching across a wide page. Squares never grow past 15 px, so a wide
container leaves empty space on the right.

### Thresholds

`Thresholds` holds the upper bounds of levels one to three; only the first three values are used. A count of zero is
level 0 with no tint, a count up to the first bound is level 1, a count up to the second is level 2, a count up to the
third is level 3, and a count above the third bound is level 4.

When `Thresholds` is not set, the control derives the bounds from the busiest day in the range: the first bound is a
quarter of that day's count (rounded up, at least 1), the second is half of it (at least 2), and the third is three
quarters of it (at least 3). A year with one exceptional day of 31 deploys therefore sets the bounds at 8, 16 and 24,
and most ordinary days fall into level 1. Set fixed bounds when the reader compares years or teams, because derived
bounds change with every data set.

```csharp
workouts.Thresholds = [1, 2, 3];
```

Setting `Thresholds` also fixes the legend ranges. `EffectiveThresholds` returns the three bounds in use.

### Selecting a day

`SelectedDate` is the selected day and is two-way. A selection ring glides to the day and fades in where it first
lands. `DateSelected` reports a day chosen with a click, Enter or Space. Its arguments carry the `Date`, the day's
`Count` and its `Level` from 0 (none) to 4 (busiest), so the handler can show a summary or open a detail view without
looking up the data again.

```csharp
heatmap.DateSelected += (_, e) => selected.Text =
    $"Selected {e.Date:MMM d, yyyy}: {e.Count} contributions (level {e.Level})";
```

Setting `SelectedDate` in code moves the ring but does not raise `DateSelected`, because the event reports a choice the
person made. Use the property to restore a selection, for example when the page reopens, and use the event to react to
the choice.

### Binding to a view model

The view model owns the days, the period and the selected date. Use a view model with
CommunityToolkit.Mvvm style properties, and bind the heatmap to them.

```csharp
public sealed record DailyDeploys(DateOnly Date, double Deploys);

public interface IDeployHistory
{
    Task<IReadOnlyList<DailyDeploys>> DailyCountsAsync(int year);
}

public partial class ActivityViewModel : ObservableObject
{
    private readonly IDeployHistory _history;

    public ActivityViewModel(IDeployHistory history) => _history = history;

    [ObservableProperty]
    private ObservableCollection<ActivityDay> _days = [];

    [ObservableProperty]
    private string _periodLabel = "the last year";

    [ObservableProperty]
    private DateOnly? _selectedDate;

    [ObservableProperty]
    private string _selectedSummary = "Select a day to see its deploys.";

    [RelayCommand]
    private async Task ShowYearAsync(string year)
    {
        var counts = await _history.DailyCountsAsync(int.Parse(year));
        Days = new ObservableCollection<ActivityDay>(
            counts.Select(c => new ActivityDay(c.Date, c.Deploys)));
        PeriodLabel = year;
    }

    partial void OnSelectedDateChanged(DateOnly? value)
    {
        SelectedSummary = value is { } date
            ? $"{date:MMM d, yyyy} is selected."
            : "Select a day to see its deploys.";
    }
}
```

```xml
<StackPanel Width="620" Spacing="16">
    <arc:ActivityHeatmap Label="Production deploys"
                         Period="{Binding PeriodLabel}"
                         UnitOne="deploy"
                         UnitOther="deploys"
                         ItemsSource="{Binding Days}"
                         SelectedDate="{Binding SelectedDate, Mode=TwoWay}">
        <arc:ActivityHeatmap.Actions>
            <arc:Button Content="2025" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small"
                        Command="{Binding ShowYearCommand}" CommandParameter="2025" />
        </arc:ActivityHeatmap.Actions>
    </arc:ActivityHeatmap>
    <TextBlock Text="{Binding SelectedSummary}"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextMuted}" />
</StackPanel>
```

- `ItemsSource` is one-way: the heatmap reads the collection and rebuilds the grid. An `ObservableCollection` is watched,
  so changes to it are reflected at once. Assigning a new collection, as the command does, is the simplest way to
  refresh a whole year.
- `SelectedDate` is two-way. A selection made on the grid updates the view model, and a value set by the view model moves
  the ring without raising `DateSelected`.
- `Period` and `Label` are plain properties; bind them in the same update as `ItemsSource` so the summary and the
  grid's name never describe different data.
- `DateSelected` is an event, not a command. Attach it in code-behind, where the handler can read the `Date`, `Count`
  and `Level` of the event args and copy the values into the view model's own properties.

### Data shape and performance

`ActivityDay` holds a `DateOnly` and a `double` count. The control builds one dense entry per calendar day between the
earliest and latest date, so missing days are zero and do not need rows. Two days with the same date add together, and
negative counts count as zero. A year is about 370 squares, which the grid draws in one pass; a multi-year range
multiplies the columns and scrolls sideways.

When the source is not `ActivityDay`, read each item with `DateSelector` and `CountSelector`, or with
`DateMemberBinding` and `CountMemberBinding`. The member binding reads a `DateOnly`, a `DateTime` or a string in
`yyyy-MM-dd` form. `DateSelector` wins over `DateMemberBinding` when both are set.

```csharp
var heatmap = new ActivityHeatmap
{
    ItemsSource = rows,
    DateSelector = row => DateOnly.ParseExact(((Row)row).Day, "yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
    CountSelector = row => ((Row)row).Deploys
};
```

Set `Culture` when dates or numbers must follow the reader's language. The total uses `#,0.##` in that culture, so a
fractional count keeps up to two decimals and a large total gets the local grouping separator.

Update the data by replacing the collection or by changing items in a collection the heatmap watches. A calendar
summarizes days, so refresh it on a schedule that matches how the data changes, such as once per page load or once per
hour, rather than on every event.

### Example: deploy frequency for a platform team

measure and the period, the unit nouns read as "deploys", and the weeks start on Monday, the first day of the
team's working week. The export button sits beside the summary as an action. Weekend days are mostly quiet, so the
weekday rhythm is visible without any extra labels.

### Content guidelines

- **Label**: name the measure and the period in sentence case, such as "Production deploys, last five weeks". The label
  is the grid's accessible name, so it must make sense without the picture.
- **Period**: a short phrase that finishes "contributions in ...": "2025", "the last six months", "Q3 2026". Leave it
  out only when the label already states the period.
- **Units**: set `UnitOne` and `UnitOther` to the nouns people use for the count, such as "deploy" and "deploys" or
  "workout" and "workouts". Avoid generic words such as "items" when the count has a precise meaning.
- **Thresholds**: when you set them, describe them in the caption or a note, such as "Darker squares mean more
  deploys", so a reader knows that the tints are relative to the bounds.
- **Actions**: keep to one or two small buttons with short verbs or years, such as "Export" or "2025".

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| Activity data | Production deploys, last five weeks |
| 2025 | Contributions in 2025 |
| 1 contributions | 1 contribution (the noun follows the total) |
| Heatmap of stuff | Workouts, last six months |
| Click here for details | Select a day to see its deploys |

### Best practices

**Do**

- Set `Label` and `Period` for every heatmap. The label is the only name a screen reader has for the grid, and the
  period completes the summary, so a reader never sees a bare total.
- Pass a whole calendar year, or a fixed range, for each view. A grid that starts on a random date makes two years hard
  to compare.
- Set `Thresholds` when comparing periods or teams. Derived bounds follow the busiest day, so the same count can be
  level 2 in one year and level 1 in another.
- Set `FirstDayOfWeek` to match the audience's calendar, Monday for working weeks and Sunday for personal activity.
- Use `DateSelected` to open the detail for a day. The event carries the date, count and level, so the handler does not
  need to look the day up again.

**Avoid**

- Using the heatmap for exact values. The squares show a tint, not a number, so a reader who needs the exact count must
  select the day or see a table.
- Passing several years in one heatmap. The grid becomes very wide and the reader must scroll sideways to see the
  latest weeks.
- Attaching a good or bad meaning to the tints. The levels only rank how busy a day was, and a single accent hue is
  not a status signal, so explain the meaning in the label or the caption instead.
- Refreshing the data on a timer that is shorter than the data changes. The totals and tints change daily, so frequent
  updates move the page without adding information.
- Placing a heatmap in a narrow column. At 440 px or less the legend caption shows only the count, and once the squares
  reach their 9 px minimum the grid scrolls sideways from the newest week, so give it the full width of its panel.

### Common questions

**Why does the grid start in the middle of a week?** The grid starts at the earliest date in the data and fills the
first week column from `FirstDayOfWeek`. Days before the start in that first column are empty, so the first square
can fall on any row.

**Why are most of my days the same light tint?** The default bounds are quarters of the busiest day. One outlier day
sets high bounds, so most ordinary days land in level 1. Set `Thresholds` to fixed values that match the typical range.

**Why does setting `SelectedDate` not trigger my handler?** `DateSelected` fires only for a choice made with a click,
Enter or Space. Setting the property moves the ring without raising the event, so update your own state in the setter
or in the view model when you need it.

**How do I show which days sit at one level?** The legend does this already. Hover or focus a swatch to preview its
level, and click a swatch to pin it. The caption then counts the days at that level, such as "96 days", followed by the
level's range when the legend is wider than 440 px, and the matching squares stand out.

## API reference

### ActivityHeatmap

A contribution-style calendar (Arc "Activity heatmap"): one square per day, weeks as columns, four accent tints for how busy a day was. Cells wave in once on first view; a single tooltip glides between cells on hover or keyboard focus; a new range recolors the grid in a diagonal sweep instead of redrawing it; the legend previews (hover, focus) or pins (click) one level. ↑ / ↓ move by day, ← / → by week, Home / End to the ends, Enter / Space select.

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ItemsSource` | `IEnumerable?` | `null` | Defines the `ItemsSource` property. |
| `DateSelector` | `Func<object, DateOnly>?` | `null` | Defines the `DateSelector` property. |
| `CountSelector` | `Func<object, double>?` | `null` | Defines the `CountSelector` property. |
| `Label` | `string?` | `null` | Defines the `Label` property. |
| `Period` | `string?` | `null` | Defines the `Period` property. |
| `UnitOne` | `string` | `"contribution"` | Defines the `UnitOne` property. |
| `UnitOther` | `string` | `"contributions"` | Defines the `UnitOther` property. |
| `Thresholds` | `IReadOnlyList<double>?` | `null` | Defines the `Thresholds` property. |
| `FirstDayOfWeek` | `DayOfWeek` | `Sunday` | Defines the `FirstDayOfWeek` property. |
| `Culture` | `CultureInfo?` | `null` | Defines the `Culture` property. |
| `SelectedDate` | `DateOnly?` | `null` | Defines the `SelectedDate` property. |
| `Actions` | `object?` | `null` | Defines the `Actions` property. |

| Event | Arguments | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DateSelected` | `ActivityHeatmapDateSelectedEventArgs` | Raised when a day is chosen with a click, Enter or Space. |

Derives from `Control`: every member of `Control` works as well.

### ActivityDay

One day of an `ActivityHeatmap`.

## Accessibility

- `Label` names the grid, such as "Contributions in 2025". The summary completes the name with the total and the period.
- The up and down arrow keys move one day, and the left and right arrow keys move one week. Home and End go to the first
  and last day, and Enter or Space selects the focused day.
- Escape hides the tooltip. A single tooltip glides between the days, and it is not repeated for each square.
- Each day is a named grid cell. The cells are hidden from assistive technology as drawing, and the summary and the grid
  structure carry the information.
- The total is announced in a status region, and the day under the pointer or the focus is announced politely. The
  legend shows a caption with the number of days at the highlighted level, so a level is not identified by its color
  alone.
- The focused day is read as its count, weekday and date, for example "31 contributions, Wednesday, December 31, 2025".
- The summary is the help text of the whole control, so a reader who opens the control's description hears the total
  and the period first.

### Keyboard

The grid takes focus as one tab stop. When it gains focus from the keyboard, the newest day is focused first.

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | Move focus into the grid on the newest day, then to the legend or the next control |
| `Up` / `Down` | Move one day earlier or later |
| `Left` / `Right` | Move one week earlier or later |
| `Home` / `End` | Move to the first or the last day of the range |
| `Enter` / `Space` | Select the focused day and raise `DateSelected` |
| `Escape` | Hide the tooltip |

The legend is a second tab stop. `Left` and `Right` move between the five swatches and preview their level, `Home` and
`End` go to the first and last swatch, `Enter` or `Space` pins a level, and `Escape` clears the preview. Pressing `Enter`
or `Space` on the pinned level again removes the pin. `Escape` clears a preview but keeps a pin.

## Motion

- On first view the cells wave in once, with the total duration capped so that a large grid stays quick.
- A new year or range recolors the grid in a diagonal sweep, with the cells staggered by column.
- The tooltip glides between cells on a snappy spring, and its text rolls to the new day.
- The total counts to its new value on a smooth spring.
- Reduced motion removes the wave, the sweep and the glide, and uses a short fade of 160 ms. Off jumps to the final state.

| Change | Full | Reduced | Off |
|---|---|---|---|
| First view | Cells wave in once, the total duration is capped | Short fade of 160 ms | Immediate |
| New range or year | Diagonal sweep, staggered by column | Short fade of 160 ms | Immediate |
| Tooltip moves to another day | Glides between cells on a snappy spring | Short fade of 160 ms | Immediate |

Keep the sweep for changes of range, such as a year switch. The wave runs once on first view, so a page that reloads
the same year gains nothing from it.

## Related

- `BarChart` for exact comparison between periods.
- `Calendar` for choosing a date.
- `LineChart` for a trend of a value over time.
- `Sparkline` for a compact trend beside a value.

| Component | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `BarChart` | The reader compares exact values across days, weeks or categories |
| `Calendar` | A person picks a date for input, such as a booking or a due date |
| `LineChart` | A continuous value over time matters more than the rhythm of single days |
| `Sparkline` | A small trend sits beside a number in a table row or a KPI card |
| `DatePicker` | A form field needs a single date, not a view of activity |

# Animated counter

> Give changing totals a clear sense of movement.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/animated-counter

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.AnimatedCounterRollingDigitsDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="20">
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:AnimatedCounter x:Name="Revenue" Label="Revenue" Value="48250" Prefix="$" />
            <arc:AnimatedCounter x:Name="Users" Label="Active users" Value="999" />
            <arc:AnimatedCounter x:Name="Rate" Label="Conversion" Value="3.42" Decimals="2" Suffix="%" />
        </WrapPanel>
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="Increase" Variant="Secondary" Click="OnIncreaseClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Decrease" Variant="Secondary" Click="OnDecreaseClick" />
        </WrapPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class AnimatedCounterRollingDigitsDemo : UserControl
{
    private readonly Random _random = new(7);

    public AnimatedCounterRollingDigitsDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnIncreaseClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Revenue.Value += _random.Next(100, 4000);
        Users.Value += _random.Next(1, 40);
        Rate.Value = Math.Round(Rate.Value + _random.NextDouble(), 2);
    }

    private void OnDecreaseClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Revenue.Value = Math.Max(0, Revenue.Value - _random.Next(100, 4000));
        Users.Value = Math.Max(0, Users.Value - _random.Next(1, 40));
        Rate.Value = Math.Max(0, Math.Round(Rate.Value - _random.NextDouble(), 2));
    }
}
```

## When to use

`AnimatedCounter` shows one number on its own, large enough to read at a glance, and rolls its digits to the new value
when the number changes. It works like the odometer of a car: only the digit columns that changed turn, so a reader can
see that a figure moved and by roughly how much, without the page flashing or the number jumping to a new width.

- **Headline totals on a billing overview**: monthly recurring revenue or the number of active subscriptions at the top
  of a SaaS admin console. The roll tells the finance team that the figure refreshed, even when they are not looking at
  the chart below it.
- **Live counters in an operations console**: open incidents, queued jobs or signed-in sessions that change while the
  page is open. Set the new value when the data arrives, and the digits move from the old value to the new one.
- **Statistics that count up on first view**: a landing page or a quarterly report where "128,400 teams" should roll up
  from zero as the reader scrolls to it, with `AnimateOnView` doing the work.
- **Balances and prices in fintech and checkout**: a wallet balance that changes after a payment, or a running total in
  a cart. Fix `Decimals` so the number keeps its width as it changes and the layout does not shift.
- **Rates and percentages in a growth dashboard**: a conversion rate or a retention figure with `Suffix="%"`, shown
  beside the total it belongs to, so the reader sees the headline and the rate together.

## When not to use

- **A number that needs a card, a label and a change indicator**: use `MetricCard`, which places a counter like this one
  inside a card with its trend.
- **Text that changes instead of a number**: use `TextMorph`, which animates words and phrases rather than digit columns.
- **The headline of a chart**: `BarChart`, `LineChart` and the other chart controls update their own headline values, so
  a separate counter next to a chart repeats the same number.
- **Many numbers in rows**: use `Table`. Each counter animates its own digit columns, which suits a few
  headline numbers, not a column of values that people scan and sort.
- **A value that a person types or edits**: use `NumberField` or `MoneyInput`. A counter only displays a number; it has no
  input, no parsing and no validation.

## Usage

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Revenue"
                         Prefix="$"
                         Value="{Binding Revenue}" />
</UserControl>
```

`AnimatedCounter` derives from Avalonia's `TemplatedControl`. Its template is a label above a `RollingDigits` primitive
from the Arc core, which does the digit work. The counter adds the label, the affixes and the reveal on first view, and
its theme sets the font, size, weight and foreground of the number, so you rarely need to set those yourself. Because
it is a template, you can restyle the counter with a `ControlTheme` in the same way as any other Arc control.

`Value` takes the raw number, not a formatted string. The counter formats it with `Decimals`, `CultureName`, `Prefix`
and `Suffix`, so the same value can show "$48,250" with en-US or "48.250" with de-DE, without changing the data.

### Anatomy

1. **Label** (`Label`): a line above the number, in the muted text color, in the extra-small type size with regular
   weight. It sits 8 px above the digits. It is hidden when `Label` is null, and it swaps with a short blur when its text
   changes.
2. **Digits** (`Value`): the number itself, drawn by `RollingDigits` in the display font family at the 3XL type size with
   medium weight, in the foreground color. The counter is left aligned by default.
3. **Prefix** (`Prefix`): text before the digits, in the same style, such as a currency sign. It is part of the rolling
   text, so it moves with the number and keeps its position when the width changes.
4. **Suffix** (`Suffix`): text after the digits, such as a percent sign or a unit. Like the prefix, it is part of the
   rolling text.

The counter has no border, background or padding of its own. Put it in a card, a row or a header and let the layout
supply the surface, so it fits the page it sits on.

### Decimals and suffix

`Decimals` fixes the number of digits after the decimal point (default 0). Negative values count as 0. Fix it to the
precision the reader needs: a conversion rate shows two decimals on every update, so the width stays the same and the
digits roll in place.

```xml
<arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Conversion" Value="{Binding Conversion}" Decimals="2" Suffix="%" />
```

Use `Suffix` for a unit or a symbol that follows the number, and keep it short. A longer phrase belongs in the label,
where it can wrap and where it does not roll with the digits.

### Updating the value

Set `Value` to the new total. Only the digit columns that changed turn, in the direction the number moved, so an
increase reads as an upward roll and a decrease as a downward roll.

```csharp
revenue.Value += random.Next(100, 4000);
rate.Value = Math.Round(rate.Value + random.NextDouble(), 2);
```

Keep the value in the unit the reader sees. Pass 48250 for "$48,250" and let `Prefix` add the sign, rather than
passing a formatted string, which the counter cannot roll.

### Reveal on view

`AnimateOnView` rolls every digit up from zero the first time 60% of the counter is visible. After that the counter
shows its value and updates as usual, so a figure that changes later only rolls from its old value to the new one.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.AnimatedCounterRevealOnViewDemo">
    <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Rolled up on first view" Value="128400" AnimateOnView="True" />
</UserControl>
```

```xml
<arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Rolled up on first view" Value="{Binding Visitors}" AnimateOnView="True" />
```

Use the reveal for a statistic that is the reason for a section, such as the number of customers on a landing page. It
is wasted on a counter in a toolbar that the reader sees constantly, where the roll would only repeat on every page
load.

### Driving it from data

The counter displays what it is given, so the data source owns the number, the refresh schedule and the rounding. The
view model holds the raw value and the counter binds to it one way.

```csharp
public sealed record BillingSummary(double Mrr, double Subscriptions, double Conversion);

public interface IBillingReports
{
    Task<BillingSummary> GetSummaryAsync(DateOnly asOf);
}

public partial class BillingOverviewViewModel : ObservableObject
{
    private readonly IBillingReports _reports;

    public BillingOverviewViewModel(IBillingReports reports) => _reports = reports;

    [ObservableProperty]
    private double _recurringRevenue;

    [ObservableProperty]
    private double _activeSubscriptions;

    [ObservableProperty]
    private double _conversionPercent;

    public async Task RefreshAsync()
    {
        var summary = await _reports.GetSummaryAsync(DateOnly.FromDateTime(DateTime.Today));
        RecurringRevenue = summary.Mrr;
        ActiveSubscriptions = summary.Subscriptions;
        ConversionPercent = Math.Round(summary.Conversion * 100, 2);
    }
}
```

```xml
<StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="32">
    <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Monthly recurring revenue" Value="{Binding RecurringRevenue}" Prefix="$" />
    <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Active subscriptions" Value="{Binding ActiveSubscriptions}" />
    <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Conversion" Value="{Binding ConversionPercent}" Decimals="2" Suffix="%" />
</StackPanel>
```

- Round the value in the view model when the business rule needs a rounded number, because the counter only rounds
  for display. The reader then sees exactly the number your rule produced.
- Refresh on a schedule that matches the data, such as once per page load or once every 30 seconds for a live count.
  A counter that changes several times a second is hard to read, so batch the updates.
- Keep the source of the number in the view model, where tests can read it, and let the counter only display it.

### Formatting and culture

`CultureName` sets the culture for the grouping separator and the decimal separator. It defaults to `en-US`, so the
output matches on the server and on the client, which matters for a number that appears in an exported report. Set it to
the reader's culture when the page is localized, and keep the default for fixed reports.

```xml
<arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Users" Value="{Binding Users}" CultureName="de-DE" />
```

The culture changes only the separators and the digits the counter draws. The prefix and the suffix are text you supply,
so write a currency sign for the culture you use, such as "€" after the number for German readers, and check that the
sign and the number order match the culture.

### Using motion with restraint

The roll is a good signal when a number changed because of an event the reader cares about: a payment arrived, a session
started, a rate moved. It is a distraction when a number changes on a timer and nothing depends on it. If several
counters roll at once on the same screen, the eye has to pick among them, so animate the one that matters most and
leave the rest as static numbers. Motion on the first view should happen once per page, not on every tab switch.

Reduced motion replaces each new value at once, so the figure stays readable for readers who turn off animation. The
information is the same; only the roll is removed.

### Example: billing overview headline figures

The header of a billing overview in an admin console for October 2026. Three figures sit side by side: the revenue, the
active subscriptions and the conversion rate. The revenue carries a currency prefix, the rate has two decimals and a
percent suffix, and each figure has a short label above it. The counters are the headline; the detail lives in the
tables below, which is why the counters are kept to three.

![Three headline figures for a billing overview: revenue, subscriptions and conversion](https://docs.tkcode.si/shots/Docs/Charts/AnimatedCounter/images/BillingFigures.webp)

```xml
<StackPanel Width="620" Spacing="16">
    <TextBlock Text="Billing overview, October 2026"
               FontSize="14"
               FontWeight="Medium"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Foreground}" />
    <StackPanel Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="32">
        <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Recurring revenue" Value="48250" Prefix="$" />
        <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Active subscriptions" Value="1284" />
        <arc:AnimatedCounter Label="Conversion" Value="3.42" Decimals="2" Suffix="%" />
    </StackPanel>
    <TextBlock Text="Updated 4 minutes ago"
               FontSize="12"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextMuted}" />
</StackPanel>
```

### Content guidelines

- **Label**: a short noun phrase in sentence case that names the measure, such as "Recurring revenue" or "Active
  subscriptions". The label is the context for the number, so do not leave it out on a headline counter.
- **Prefix and suffix**: a symbol or a short unit, "$", "€", "%", "ms". Put a longer unit in the label.
- **Decimals**: the precision of the business rule, not of the source data. Money usually shows 0 or 2 decimals,
  and a rate usually shows 1 or 2.
- **Period**: name the period in the label or in a caption near the counter, such as "Last 30 days" or "as of Oct 21,
  2026", because the counter shows a value without a date.

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| Revenue number | Recurring revenue |
| $ 48250 | $48,250 (use `Prefix="$"` and a formatted value) |
| Conv. | Conversion, last 30 days |
| Users (count) | Active subscriptions |
| 3.4212 % | 3.42% (use `Decimals="2"` and `Suffix="%"`) |

### Best practices

**Do**

- Fix `Decimals` to the precision of the figure. A width that changes between updates makes the neighboring content
  shift, which reads as a layout bug.
- Keep one counter per headline figure and put the detail in a table or a chart. Three or four counters in a row is the
  limit that a reader can scan.
- Give every counter a `Label`. The label is the accessible name's first part, so a screen reader hears what the number
  is, not only the number.
- Set `AnimateOnView` only on statistics that are the reason for the section, and leave it off for values that change
  on every refresh.

**Avoid**

- Passing a formatted string in `Value`. The counter needs a number to roll; "48,250" is not a value it can animate, and
  the grouping is applied for you.
- Rolling a counter on a timer that runs faster than the data changes. Constant motion without a new fact trains
  readers to ignore the number.
- Putting a counter in a dense table column or a list of many rows. Each counter animates its own digit columns, so a
  long list of them costs more than the reader gets from the motion.
- Using a counter as an input. It has no keyboard focus and no way for the reader to change the value; use an input
  control for values people edit.

### Common questions

**Why does the counter start from zero the first time?** Only `AnimateOnView` starts from zero. The counter arms itself
and rolls every digit up from zero when 60% of it becomes visible for the first time. Without `AnimateOnView` the
first value appears at once, and later changes roll from the old value to the new one.

**Why does `AnimateOnView` not run again when I scroll back?** The reveal runs once per counter. After the first time
the counter stays at its value, so a figure that changes later rolls only for the change, not for the reveal.

**How do I make the number announced to screen readers?** The counter does not announce its changes. Set
`AutomationProperties.LiveSetting="Polite"` on the element that contains the counter, so a change is read after the
current speech. Use it only for a number that changes because of an event the reader needs to know about.

**Why does the number look wrong for my locale?** The counter formats with `CultureName`, which defaults to `en-US`.
Set it to the reader's culture, and write the currency sign and its position yourself, since the prefix and suffix are
plain text.

**Can I round the value inside the counter?** Only for display. `Decimals` controls how many digits the counter shows
and it rounds the shown digits, but the stored `Value` is unchanged. Round in your data code when a business rule
needs the rounded number itself.

## API reference

### AnimatedCounter

A number that rolls digit by digit like an odometer: only changed columns turn (in the direction the whole number moved), separators slide in and out, and the label crossfades with a short rise. With `AnimateOnView` every digit rolls up from zero the first time 60% of the counter is visible.

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Value` | `double` | `0` | The number to display; changes animate the digits to the new value. |
| `Label` | `string?` | `null` | Accessible label announced before the value. |
| `Prefix` | `string?` | `null` | Text placed before the number, such as a currency sign. |
| `Suffix` | `string?` | `null` | Text placed after the number, such as a unit or percent sign. |
| `Decimals` | `int` | `0` | Digits after the decimal point (default 0); negative values count as 0. |
| `AnimateOnView` | `bool` | `false` | Roll every digit up from zero the first time the counter scrolls into view. |
| `CultureName` | `string` | `"en-US"` | Formatting culture; fixed (en-US) by default so every machine renders the same digits. |

Derives from `TemplatedControl`: every member of `TemplatedControl` works as well.

## Accessibility

- The counter is not focusable and defines no keyboard interaction, so it takes no keys.
- The full formatted text, with prefix, separators, decimals and suffix, is the name of the counter, so a reader gets the
  whole number at once. With a `Label`, the name reads as "Label: value".
- The rolling digits are hidden from assistive technology. The counter does not announce its changes by itself. To
  announce them, set `AutomationProperties.LiveSetting="Polite"` on the surrounding element.
- The label is visible text above the number, so the number has a visible context for every reader, not only for those
  who hear the name.

## Motion

- Each digit column turns in the direction the whole number moved, and wraps between 9 and 0.
- When the number of digits changes, the new column and the separator slide in or out, and the width eases to fit. The
  neighboring content shifts slightly with it.
- With `AnimateOnView`, the roll starts once 60% of the counter is visible, and the digits start with a slight stagger.
- Reduced motion replaces the new value at once, without rolling. Off jumps to the final state.

| Change | Full | Reduced | Off |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Value` changes | Digit columns turn in the direction of the change | The new digits appear at once | Immediate |
| Number of digits changes | The new column and separator slide in, the width eases to fit | Immediate | Immediate |
| First view with `AnimateOnView` | Digits roll up from zero, with a slight stagger | The final value appears at once | Immediate |

## Related

- `MetricCard` for a number inside a card with its label and change.
- `Sparkline` for a number with its trend.
- `BarChart` and `LineChart` update their own headline values, so they do not need this counter.
- `TextMorph` for text that changes rather than a number.

| Component | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `MetricCard` | The number needs a card, a title and a change indicator |
| `Sparkline` | The number needs a compact trend next to it |
| `TextMorph` | The changing content is a word or a phrase, not a number |
| `NumberField` / `MoneyInput` | The person types or edits the number |
| `Table` | Many numbers are shown in rows that people scan and sort |

# Ridgeline

> Overlapping distributions, one ridge per group: hover to lift a ridge and read its quartiles, switch datasets and every curve morphs.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/ridgeline

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.RidgelineDistributionsByMonthDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="16">
        <arc:Ridgeline x:Name="Chart"
                       Label="Daily highs in Zurich"
                       Unit="°C"
                       DomainMinimum="-5"
                       DomainMaximum="35" />
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="Zurich" Variant="Secondary" Click="OnZurichClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Lisbon" Variant="Secondary" Click="OnLisbonClick" />
        </WrapPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class RidgelineDistributionsByMonthDemo : UserControl
{
    private static readonly string[] s_months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"];

    private static readonly RidgelineSeries[] s_zurich = Highs([3, 5, 10, 14, 19, 22, 25, 24, 20, 14, 8, 4], 3.2, 4);

    private static readonly RidgelineSeries[] s_lisbon = Highs([15, 16, 19, 20, 22, 26, 28, 29, 27, 23, 18, 15], 2.4, 9);

    public RidgelineDistributionsByMonthDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        Chart.ItemsSource = s_zurich;
    }

    // Replace the label and the groups together; every curve morphs from its current shape to the new one.
    private void OnZurichClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) => Show("Daily highs in Zurich", s_zurich);

    private void OnLisbonClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) => Show("Daily highs in Lisbon", s_lisbon);

    private void Show(string label, RidgelineSeries[] months)
    {
        Chart.Label = label;
        Chart.ItemsSource = months;
    }

    /// <summary>Daily highs per month around a seasonal mean (deterministic, normal noise).</summary>
    private static RidgelineSeries[] Highs(double[] means, double spread, int seed)
    {
        var random = new Random(seed);
        double Normal() => Math.Sqrt(-2 * Math.Log(1 - random.NextDouble())) * Math.Cos(2 * Math.PI * random.NextDouble());
        return means.Select((mean, month) => new RidgelineSeries(s_months[month].ToLowerInvariant(), s_months[month],
            Enumerable.Range(0, 30).Select(_ => Math.Round(mean + Normal() * spread * (month is 0 or 11 ? 1.3 : 1), 1)).ToArray())).ToArray();
    }
}
```

## When to use

`Ridgeline` compares the shape of several distributions side by side. Each group is one ridge: a smoothed density curve
drawn over the row above it, so the reader sees spread, skew and a second hump that a single average would hide. It fits
an operations or analytics page where the question is how the groups differ in their distribution, not only in their
average.

- **Response times by region** on a status or observability page. Three ridges show that Asia Pacific has a second group
  of slow responses near 250 ms that the median alone would hide.
- **Daily highs by month** in a weather or energy-demand dashboard. The ridges show the seasonal shift and whether the
  spread widens in winter.
- **Order values by customer segment** in an e-commerce review. A segment with two humps (small single items and bulk
  orders) reads as two ridges' worth of shape, not a misleading mean.
- **Resolution times by team** in a support or CRM report. The long tail of slow tickets is visible on each team's row.
- **Delivery times by carrier** in a logistics console, where the on-time share matters more than the average.

## When not to use

- **One summary number per group**, such as average revenue by region: use `BarChart`, which compares the values exactly.
- **Few observations per group**: a curve drawn from a handful of values is guesswork. Use a table of summaries, or
  `BarChart` for the summary numbers, when a group has fewer than about 20 values.
- **A change of one value over time**: use `LineChart`, where the x axis is time.
- **Exact comparison of a few values**: use `BarChart` or a table. Ridges show shape, not precise differences.
- **Parts of a whole**, such as traffic share by source: use `DonutChart`.
- **Density over days and hours**, such as activity by weekday and hour: use `ActivityHeatmap`, which shows each cell as
  a count.

## Usage

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:Ridgeline Label="Daily highs in Zurich"
                   Unit="°C"
                   DomainMinimum="-5"
                   DomainMaximum="35"
                   ItemsSource="{Binding Months}" />
</UserControl>
```

Each `RidgelineSeries` is one group: an `Id`, a `Label` and its raw `Values`. The chart computes a density for each group
and draws the ridges from top to bottom in the order of the series. `Ridgeline` derives from Avalonia's `Control`, not
from a templated chart, so the whole box takes the pointer and the ridges, labels and scale are drawn by the control
itself. It takes keyboard focus only when it has observations to read.

### Anatomy

1. **Row labels** (`RidgelineSeries.Label`): drawn in the left gutter, 52 px wide (36 px when the chart is narrower than
   420 px), above each row's baseline. A label that does not fit is shortened.
2. **Ridges**: one filled curve per group, sampled at 96 points on a domain shared by all groups. Each ridge is tinted by
   its median when `IsTinted` is on, and drawn in the first series color when it is off.
3. **Rows and overlap**: each row is 30 px high by default (`RowHeight`). The tallest ridge rises 2.4 row heights into the
   rows above (`Overlap`), so the top ridges are not clipped.
4. **Value axis**: a 28 px band under the last row, with tick labels about 72 px apart, formatted with `Unit`.
5. **Median scale** (`IsTinted`): a "Median" label, the lowest and highest values, and five color swatches, right aligned
   under the axis.
6. **Lifted ridge**: a copy drawn above the others, raised 6 px, with its middle half shaded and its median marked by a
   short stroke.
7. **Tooltip**: the series label, the median, the middle half and the range, plus the share of values at or below the
   reading cursor once it moves. It is at least 170 px wide and
   stays inside the chart.

### Datasets

Replace `ItemsSource` to switch the dataset. Every curve morphs from its current shape to the new one, and the ridge
order stays the same.

```csharp
// Keep each dataset as an array and assign the one the person chose.
chart.ItemsSource = selectedDataset == "zurich" ? zurichMonths : lisbonMonths;
```

Ridges are matched by `Id`, so a group that exists in both datasets with the same id morphs into its new shape. A group
that is new appears on its own row.

### Items and value formats

Add groups through `Items` when they are created in code, or bind `ItemsSource` for a view model. `ValueFormatter` sets
the format for the axis ticks, the median scale, the summary and the tooltip.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.RidgelineUntintedDemo">
    <arc:Ridgeline x:Name="Chart"
                   Label="Response time by region"
                   IsTinted="False"
                   RowHeight="36"
                   Overlap="1.8" />
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class RidgelineUntintedDemo : UserControl
{
    public RidgelineUntintedDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        Chart.ValueFormatter = v => $"{v:0} ms";

        // Three regions whose slow responses form a second hump (deterministic).
        var random = new Random(2);
        foreach (var (id, label, center, tail) in new[] { ("eu", "Europe", 120.0, 30.0), ("us", "Americas", 160.0, 45.0), ("ap", "Asia Pacific", 210.0, 70.0) })
        {
            Chart.Items.Add(new RidgelineSeries(id, label, Enumerable.Range(0, 80)
                .Select(i => center + (random.NextDouble() - 0.5) * tail + (i % 9 == 0 ? tail * 1.6 : 0)).ToArray()));
        }
    }
}
```

### Overlap and smoothness

`Overlap` sets how far the ridges rise into the row above, as a multiple of the row height. `RowHeight` sets the height of
one row. `Bandwidth` sets the smoothing in the units of the values: a larger value gives a smoother, more general shape,
and a smaller value keeps more of the bumps in the data. By default each group uses Silverman's rule of thumb, which
picks a bandwidth from that group's own spread and count.

```xml
<arc:Ridgeline Label="Latency" Overlap="2.4" RowHeight="30" Bandwidth="4" ItemsSource="{Binding Regions}" />
```

### Tint and domain

`IsTinted` colors each ridge by its median, from a light tint to the first series color, and shows the median scale under
the axis. Turn it off when the groups should read as one family, or when the color would suggest a ranking that is not
the point of the chart. `DomainMinimum` and `DomainMaximum` fix the value axis, so it does not move when the dataset
changes. Leave them unset (NaN) and the axis covers the data with room for the smoothing, rounded to nice steps.

```xml
<arc:Ridgeline Label="Latency" IsTinted="False" DomainMinimum="0" DomainMaximum="300" ItemsSource="{Binding Regions}" />
```

### Reading a ridge

`ActiveId` is the lifted ridge, and it is two-way. `ActiveIdChanged` reports each change, with the lifted series in
`Series`.

```csharp
chart.ActiveIdChanged += (_, e) => readout.Text = e.Series is null
    ? string.Empty
    : $"{e.Series.Label}: {e.Series.Values.Count} observations";
```

The tooltip and the accessible text carry the median, the middle half and the range. If the page needs its own figures,
compute them from `Series` in the handler, for example a 95th percentile for a latency panel.

### Binding to a view model

With CommunityToolkit.Mvvm the view model owns the groups and the selected group. Each group is a `RidgelineSeries`,
and the view model replaces the array for a new dataset. The chart keeps the lifted group in `ActiveId`.

```csharp
public partial class LatencyViewModel : ObservableObject
{
    [ObservableProperty]
    private RidgelineSeries[] _regions = [];

    [ObservableProperty]
    private string? _activeRegion;

    public void Load(IReadOnlyDictionary<string, double[]> samplesByRegion)
    {
        Regions = samplesByRegion
            .Select(pair => new RidgelineSeries(pair.Key, pair.Key, pair.Value))
            .ToArray();
    }
}
```

```xml
<arc:Ridgeline Label="Response time by region"
               Unit="ms"
               ItemsSource="{Binding Regions}"
               ActiveId="{Binding ActiveRegion, Mode=TwoWay}" />
```

- `ActiveId` is two-way: the chart writes it when a ridge is lifted, and the view model can lift a ridge from code.
- Items that are not `RidgelineSeries` work when you set `KeySelector`, `LabelSelector` and `ValuesSelector`, or the
  matching member bindings (`KeyMemberBinding`, `LabelMemberBinding` and `ValuesMemberBinding`). The selectors win when
  both are set.
- Compiled bindings need `x:DataType` on the view; the examples use plain `Binding` for brevity.

### Data shape and performance

Pass raw observations, not a histogram. Non-finite values (NaN and infinity) are ignored. If two series share an `Id`, the
first one is drawn and the later one is dropped, so keep ids unique within a dataset.

The density is computed once per data change for each group, on the shared domain, and the animation only interpolates
the sampled curves. Keep the number of groups to about twenty, and the observations per group to at least twenty, so each
curve has a real shape. Heights share one scale: the tallest peak of all groups rises to the overlap height. A group
with more observations does not look taller. A tall, narrow ridge means that its values are concentrated.

Format values with `ValueFormatter` or `Unit`. The default format groups thousands, uses at most one decimal and a true
minus sign, then appends `Unit`, so -3 °C reads as "−3°C".

### Example: response times by region

An operations page for Acme Analytics shows how response times differ across three regions over one week. The median
alone would say that Asia Pacific is only a little slower than the Americas. The ridges show that a second group of slow
responses sits near 250 ms, which is the part the on-call engineer needs to see. The tinted ridges and the median scale
show the rank order, and the fixed domain keeps the axis still when the page is filtered to another week.

![A response time ridgeline with three regions, tinted by median, with a second slow group in Asia Pacific](https://docs.tkcode.si/shots/Docs/Charts/Ridgeline/images/ResponseTimeRidges.webp)

                            <sys:Double>196</sys:Double>
                        </collections:AvaloniaList>
                    </arc:RidgelineSeries.Values>
                </arc:RidgelineSeries>
                <arc:RidgelineSeries Id="ap" Label="APAC">
                    <arc:RidgelineSeries.Values>
                        <collections:AvaloniaList x:TypeArguments="sys:Double">
