# Payment flow

> A card payment from checkout through tokenization, authorization and the issuer's decision to settlement.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/payment-flow

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.PaymentFlowCardPaymentDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="12">
        <arc:PaymentFlow x:Name="Payment" PaymentCompleted="OnPaymentCompleted" />
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="0.5×" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnHalfSpeedClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="1×" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnNormalSpeedClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="2×" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnDoubleSpeedClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Start over" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small" Click="OnRestartClick" />
            <TextBlock x:Name="Log"
                       Text="No payments yet"
                       FontSize="13"
                       TextWrapping="Wrap"
                       VerticalAlignment="Center"
                       Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextMuted}" />
        </WrapPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class PaymentFlowCardPaymentDemo : UserControl
{
    private int _approved;
    private int _total;

    public PaymentFlowCardPaymentDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnPaymentCompleted(object? sender, PaymentCompletedEventArgs e)
    {
        _total++;
        _approved += e.Approved ? 1 : 0;
        Log.Text = $"{(e.Approved ? "Approved" : "Declined")} · {_approved} of {_total} approved";
    }

    private void OnHalfSpeedClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Payment.Speed = 0.5;
    }

    private void OnNormalSpeedClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Payment.Speed = 1;
    }

    private void OnDoubleSpeedClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Payment.Speed = 2;
    }

    private void OnRestartClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Payment.Restart();
    }
}
```

## When to use

`PaymentFlow` explains what happens between a customer pressing Pay and the merchant receiving the funds. It draws
the route of one card payment: checkout, the payment gateway that tokenizes the card, the card network, the issuing
bank that approves or declines, the response that travels back, and the settlement to the merchant account. It sits on
checkout help pages, payment documentation and onboarding screens, where the reader needs to know why a payment can be
approved or declined and when the money arrives.

- **Checkout help for a declined card**: a help article on the checkout page that explains a decline. The diagram
  shows that the issuing bank made the decision, so the customer knows to contact the bank or try another card.
- **Integration documentation for a payment provider**: a developer guide that shows the amount, currency and merchant
  as they are configured for the integration, and where the tokenization and authorization steps happen.
- **Merchant onboarding for settlement timing**: a page that explains when approved funds reach the merchant's payout
  account. The settlement path and the balance readout show the order of events without a table of timings.
- **Sales or support training**: a short explanation for support staff who answer "why was my card declined" questions,
  with the decline path shown in the danger color.
- **Product marketing on a pricing page**: a visual for a feature that handles card payments end to end, placed beside
  the description of the payment methods.

## When not to use

- **Entering a payment amount or card details**: use `MoneyInput` for an amount that a person types and a form for the
  card fields. `PaymentFlow` only illustrates the flow; it has no input.
- **Plotting payment totals over time**: use `BarChart` or `LineChart` from the Charts category for revenue, volume or
  decline rates. The balance readout in the illustration counts the story, not your ledger.
- **The live status of a real payment**: use `Alert` for a payment that failed, `Badge` for its state and `Timeline` for
  the events of one transaction. An illustration that loops cannot report that a particular payment is still pending.
- **A list of past payments**: use `DataGrid` with the amounts, dates and decline codes. A single animated example does
  not replace a searchable history.
- **A multi-step checkout the customer completes**: use `Stepper` for the steps of the checkout itself. `PaymentFlow`
  shows what happens after the customer presses Pay and does not take input.

## Usage

The story plays one payment after another. The caption under the diagram describes the current step, and the merchant
balance grows with every approved payment. The control needs no data to run, and it uses the default amount of 42,
the merchant Northwind and the card ending in 4242.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:PaymentFlow />
</UserControl>
```

`PaymentFlow` derives from `Illustration`, which derives from Avalonia's `TemplatedControl`. It takes focus, has a
`Label` for assistive technology, and uses the same frame, caption and playback button as the other system
illustrations. Each payment is a fixed sequence on the scene clock, so the same inputs always produce the same
story, and the decision the issuer makes is a value the control knows before the animation reaches it.

### Anatomy

1. **Customer** (`Labels.Customer`): the card at the top left. Its detail line shows the last four digits, for
   example "•••• 4242", and an amount badge above it shows the amount when a payment starts.
2. **Checkout** (`Labels.Checkout`): the merchant's checkout, with the merchant name (`MerchantName`) as its detail line.
   It turns to the accent color while it sends the card details, and to success or danger when the payment ends.
3. **Gateway** (`Labels.Gateway`, `Labels.GatewayDetail`): the payment gateway that tokenizes the card. A "Tokenized"
   badge with a lock icon sits above it while the gateway holds the token.
4. **Card network** (`Labels.Network`, `Labels.NetworkDetail`): the network that carries the authorization request.
5. **Issuing bank** (`Labels.Issuer`, `Labels.IssuerDetail`): the bank below the card network. Its busy ring turns on
   while it checks funds and risk, and a badge below it reads "Approved" or "Declined" with its icon.
6. **Merchant account** (`Labels.Merchant`, `Labels.MerchantDetail`): the payout account below the checkout. A balance
   readout beneath it (`Labels.Balance`) shows the amount in the currency, and a "+ amount" badge shows each settlement.
7. **Settlement line**: a dashed line from the gateway that turns left to the merchant account. It carries the funds
   only for approved payments.
8. **Caption line** and **play button**: the same controls as the other illustrations. The button is hidden in the
   still poster.

The scene is 844 by 270 units and scales to the width the control is given. The nodes are 150 by 52 units with the
12 px corner radius of the token, and the frame has 20 px of padding on the sides and top and 14 px at the bottom. A
request travels on the upper lane of each connection and the response on the lower lane, so the two never overlap.

### Amount, currency and merchant

`Amount` is a `decimal` and defaults to 42. `Currency` is an ISO code and defaults to USD; an empty value falls back to
USD. `MerchantName` names the merchant at checkout and `CardLast4` shows the last four digits of the card.

The illustration formats money for the currency. USD, EUR and GBP show their symbol with two decimals, JPY and KRW show
their symbol with no decimals, CNY and INR show their symbol with two decimals, and other codes show the ISO code and a
space before the amount, such as "CHF 42.00". Thousands are grouped, and the number always uses the invariant culture,
so "1,284.00" reads the same on every machine.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.PaymentFlowAmountAndMerchantDemo">
    <arc:PaymentFlow Amount="129.90"
                     Currency="EUR"
                     MerchantName="Atelier"
                     CardLast4="0119"
                     DeclineEvery="0" />
</UserControl>
```

```xml
<arc:PaymentFlow Amount="129.90"
                 Currency="EUR"
                 MerchantName="Atelier"
                 CardLast4="0119"
                 DeclineEvery="0" />
```

Set `Amount` and `Currency` from the same order that the checkout charges, so the badge shown on the diagram matches
the amount the customer sees. The diagram does not convert currencies, and the balance readout is in the currency of
`Currency` even when the merchant account holds another one.

### Declines

`DeclineEvery` declines every N-th payment. The default is 4, so the fourth, eighth and twelfth payments of the story
are declined. Set it to 0 to approve every payment, and use a value of 1 to decline every payment. Negative values are
treated as 0.

```xml
<arc:PaymentFlow DeclineEvery="0" />
```

A declined payment follows the same route to the issuer. The issuer's badge reads "Declined" in the danger color, the
response travels back on the lower lane, and the caption explains the decline: "Declined: insufficient funds". The
settlement line does not light up, the merchant balance does not change, and the story stops at the step that
tells the customer to try another card.

### Labels

`Labels` takes a `PaymentFlowLabels` object with every visible word of the diagram: the node names and details, the
badges (`Approved`, `Declined`, `Paid`, `Payment failed`, `Tokenized`) and the step captions. The caption for the
payment's start is built from `Pay`, which takes the formatted amount and the merchant name, so a new label can use
both values.

```csharp
var payment = new PaymentFlow
{
    Amount = 19.00m,
    Labels = new PaymentFlowLabels
    {
        Merchant = "Shop",
        Issuer = "Issuing bank",
        Approved = "Approved",
        Declined = "Refused"
    }
};
```

Keep the labels short. The node cards hold about 16 characters on one line, and the badges sit above and below the
cards at the same width.

### Reacting to decisions

`PaymentCompleted` is raised when the issuer decides a payment. Its `PaymentCompletedEventArgs` has an `Approved`
flag and the `Amount` of the payment. `PaymentCount` gives the number of payments decided since the story started, and
`Balance` gives the merchant balance.

```csharp
payment.PaymentCompleted += (_, e) =>
    log.Text = $"{(e.Approved ? "Approved" : "Declined")} {e.Amount:0.00} · balance {payment.Balance:0.00}";
```

`Balance` rises when the settlement reaches the merchant, which is later in the story than the decision. Inside the
`PaymentCompleted` handler, `Balance` still shows the balance before this payment. Read it on a later step, or add the
amount yourself when `Approved` is true, if the log should show the new balance at the moment of the decision.

### Playback

`IsPlaying` plays and pauses the story, `Speed` scales it (0.25 to 4), and `Restart()` starts over from the first step
with the opening balance of 1,284 in the merchant account. `Step`, `StepCount` and `StepChanged` follow the steps of one
payment. The story has seven steps, and a declined payment stops at step 5, because the settlement step only runs for
approved payments.

| Step | Caption | What is shown |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | The customer pays $42.00 at Northwind (the formatted amount and merchant) | The amount badge above the customer |
| 1 | Card details are tokenized at the payment gateway | The request reaches checkout, then the gateway |
| 2 | The authorization request travels to the issuing bank | The gateway badge reads "Tokenized"; the request crosses the card network |
| 3 | The issuer checks funds and risk | The issuer's busy ring turns on |
| 4 | Approved: the response travels back, or Declined: insufficient funds | The issuer's badge and the response on the lower lane |
| 5 | The order is confirmed, or the customer is asked for another card | Checkout reads "Paid" or "Payment failed" |
| 6 | Funds settle to the merchant account (approved payments only) | The dashed settlement line and the balance readout |

```xml
<arc:PaymentFlow Speed="0.5" IsPlaying="False" />
```

A payment takes about 8.4 seconds of scene time, so the story at its default speed shows one payment in a little
under nine seconds. Stop the story with `IsPlaying` when the page explains a single payment and the animation would
compete with the text.

### Binding to a view model

In a checkout, the order owns the amount, the currency and the merchant, and the illustration only shows them. Bind
the values one way: the control never writes an amount or a currency back. `IsPlaying` is the only two-way property of
the illustration. The `PaymentCompleted` event is not a binding target, so subscribe to it in code-behind and forward
the decision to the view model.

```csharp
public partial class CheckoutViewModel : ObservableObject
{
    [ObservableProperty]
    private decimal _orderTotal = 129.90m;

    [ObservableProperty]
    private string _currency = "EUR";

    [ObservableProperty]
    private string _merchantName = "Atelier";

    [ObservableProperty]
    private string _cardLast4 = "0119";

    [ObservableProperty]
    private int _declinedCount;

    public void RecordDecision(bool approved)
    {
        if (!approved)
        {
            DeclinedCount++;
        }
    }
}
```

```xml
<arc:PaymentFlow Amount="{Binding OrderTotal}"
                 Currency="{Binding Currency}"
                 MerchantName="{Binding MerchantName}"
                 CardLast4="{Binding CardLast4}"
                 DeclineEvery="0" />
```

Subscribe to the event in code-behind, where the view model is available:

```csharp
public CheckoutView()
{
    InitializeComponent();
    Payment.PaymentCompleted += OnPaymentCompleted;
}

private void OnPaymentCompleted(object? sender, PaymentCompletedEventArgs e)
{
    ViewModel.RecordDecision(e.Approved);
}
```

Use the bindings for the values that the order already has, and keep the illustration's decline cycle for the
demonstration only. A checkout page that shows a real order should not show the animated decline cycle as if it were
the outcome of that order.

### Reduced motion

Under reduced motion (or Off) the illustration is a still frame of the approved path. Every connection is lit in the
success color, the issuer and checkout show success, the amount badge sits above the customer, and the balance readout
shows the opening balance plus the amount. The play button is hidden. Use the still frame on pages that explain the
approved path and do not need the sequence.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.PaymentFlowReducedMotionDemo">
    <arc:PaymentFlow arc:ArcMotion.Level="Reduced" />
</UserControl>
```

### Example: checkout help for a card payment

A help article on a checkout page for a design store. The order is 129.90 EUR at Atelier, the card ends in 0119, and
the illustration shows the approved path in the still frame, so the reader sees a normal payment. The text explains the
two decisions the issuer can make and the one place the reader can act, which is the card. The labels keep the
merchant's own wording where it helps, and the currency is the one the customer paid in.

![A card payment for 129.90 EUR at Atelier with the approved path and a Paid badge](https://docs.tkcode.si/shots/Docs/Illustrations/PaymentFlow/images/CardCheckout.webp)

```xml
<StackPanel Width="760" Spacing="16">
    <TextBlock Text="How your card payment is processed"
               FontSize="16"
               FontWeight="SemiBold"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Foreground}" />
    <TextBlock Text="Your bank approves or declines every payment. A decline means the bank did not approve the amount, not that the store refused the card."
               TextWrapping="Wrap"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextSecondary}" />
    <arc:PaymentFlow Label="Card payment of 129.90 EUR at Atelier"
                     Amount="129.90"
                     Currency="EUR"
                     MerchantName="Atelier"
                     CardLast4="0119"
                     DeclineEvery="0">
        <arc:PaymentFlow.Labels>
            <arc:PaymentFlowLabels Issuer="Your bank"
                                   IssuerDetail="funds · risk"
                                   Merchant="Atelier"
                                   MerchantDetail="payout account"
                                   Approved="Approved"
                                   Declined="Declined"
                                   Paid="Paid" />
        </arc:PaymentFlow.Labels>
    </arc:PaymentFlow>
</StackPanel>
```

The screenshot is the still frame of the approved path, so it shows the badges and the balance readout at their final
values. The live control plays the full sequence unless the page sets reduced motion.

### Content guidelines

Name the parties the way the reader meets them on a statement or a receipt: the merchant, the card network and "your
bank" for the issuer. Use the amount with its currency and two decimals, and keep the decision words to what the bank
actually said. Write captions in the present tense and describe the state of the payment, not the company's process.

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| Payment processed successfully | Approved |
| Your card has been rejected | Declined: insufficient funds |
| Transaction ID verified | Card details are tokenized at the payment gateway |
| Money sent to the merchant | Funds settle to the merchant account |
| 129 EUR | EUR 129.90 or 129.90 EUR, as the page's locale uses |
| Customer charged successfully | Paid |

Avoid the word "charged" for an authorization that has not settled, and do not say "refund" for a declined payment:
nothing was taken, so nothing is returned. Keep the labels short and the captions to one sentence.

### Best practices

**Do**

- Show the amount, currency and merchant that the order uses, so the diagram matches the page the customer is
  reading. A mismatched amount makes the help text read as a different payment.
- Explain on the page that the bank makes the decision. The diagram shows the issuer as the one that decides, so the
  reader does not blame the store.
- Keep the approved path on pages that describe normal payments, and use the decline cycle only in demonstrations, so
  a reader is not shown a decline for a normal order.
- Stop the story with `IsPlaying` when the page is about a single payment the reader has already made, because a loop
  in the same frame distracts from the receipt.

**Avoid**

- Presenting the sequence as the timing of a real settlement. The story takes about 8.4 seconds of scene time, and
  the settlement step shows only the order of events. Real settlement takes days and depends on the provider.
- Labelling the issuer as your company. The issuer is the customer's bank, and a diagram that names your company there
  states something you cannot know.
- Writing a count of declined payments from the illustration. `PaymentCount` and `Balance` count the story, so a page
  that shows them as sales figures reports numbers that have nothing to do with your ledger.
- Using the diagram as the only explanation of a decline. Give the customer the decline reason and the next step in
  text, because the diagram does not say which bank rule applied.

### Common questions

**Why does `Balance` not include the payment in the `PaymentCompleted` handler?** The decision happens before the
settlement reaches the merchant account, and the balance rises only when the settlement packet arrives. Read `Balance`
on a later step, or add the amount yourself after an approved decision.

**Can I make one order show a decline?** No. `DeclineEvery` counts payments in the story, and the control has no way
to receive a decision for a particular order. To explain a decline for a real order, use `Alert` or a message next to
the form that gives the bank's decline reason.

**How do I restart the story after a button press?** Call `Restart()`. It starts the first step again with the opening
balance of 1,284 and the decline counter reset, so the next payment is approved in the default cycle.

**Why does CHF show the code and not a symbol?** The illustration uses symbols for USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY, INR and
KRW. Any other currency is shown with its ISO code and a space before the amount, which avoids guessing a symbol that
the customer might not recognize.

**Can I change the labels to another language?** Yes. Set `Labels` to a `PaymentFlowLabels` object with your own
strings. `Pay` and `Balance` are functions that take the formatted values, so keep the same number of parameters as the
defaults.

## API reference

### PaymentFlow

An animated card payment: the customer pays at checkout, the gateway tokenizes the card, the authorization request travels through the card network to the issuing bank, the issuer approves or declines, the response comes back and approved payments settle to the merchant account, whose balance grows.

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Amount` | `decimal` | `42` | The amount paid (default 42). |
| `Currency` | `string` | `"USD"` | ISO currency code (default USD). |
| `MerchantName` | `string` | `"Northwind"` | The merchant shown at checkout. |
| `CardLast4` | `string` | `"4242"` | Last four digits of the card. |
| `DeclineEvery` | `int` | `4` | Every N-th payment is declined (0 never declines). |
| `Labels` | `PaymentFlowLabels` | – | Node titles, badges and caption text of the diagram; set it to rename or translate the scene. |
| `IsPlaying` | `bool` | `true` | Whether the illustration plays (two way). Paused, it holds the current frame. |
| `Speed` | `double` | `1` | Playback speed (0.25–4). |
| `Label` | `string?` | `"Payment flow illustration"` | The accessible name of the illustration. |
| `IsCaptionVisible` | `bool` | `true` | Shows the caption line under the diagram. |
| `IsPlaybackButtonVisible` | `bool` | `true` | Shows the play / pause button. |
| `Caption` | `string` | – | *Read-only.* What the current step shows (also the accessible help text). |
| `Step` | `int` | – | *Read-only.* The current step (0-based); see `StepCount`. |

| Event | Arguments | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PaymentCompleted` | `PaymentCompletedEventArgs` | Raised when the issuer decides a payment. |
| `StepChanged` | `IllustrationStepChangedEventArgs` | Raised when the story moves to another step. |

Pseudo-classes: `:playing`, `:poster`

Derives from `TemplatedControl`: every member of `TemplatedControl` works as well.

### PaymentFlowLabels

Every visible word of a `PaymentFlow` (override for another language or domain).

`PaymentCompleted` passes a `PaymentCompletedEventArgs` with these members.

| Member | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Approved` | `bool` | Whether the issuer approved the payment |
| `Amount` | `decimal` | The amount of the payment, as set in `Amount` when it was decided |

## Accessibility

- `Label` is the accessible name of the illustration. Name the flow in it, for example "Card payment for an order of
  129.90 EUR", so a screen reader user knows what the diagram is about before the caption is read.
- The illustration takes focus and shows a 2px focus ring around the frame when it is focused.
- The current caption is exposed as the help text, so the step's description is read when the control has focus.
- Caption changes are not announced, so a screen reader user does not hear the same payment repeat every few seconds.
- The decision is in text, not only in color: the issuer's badge reads "Approved" or "Declined", and the checkout
  reads "Paid" or "Payment failed". A reader who cannot see the colors still gets the outcome.
- Under reduced motion the still frame shows the approved path with its text badges and a summary caption.

### Keyboard

The illustration takes focus with Tab. Once it has focus, these keys control the story:

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | Move focus to or from the illustration |
| `Space` or `Enter` | Play or pause the story |
| `R` | Start the story over from the first step and the opening balance |

The illustration does not offer a way to choose the decision for a payment. To show a decline on demand, set
`DeclineEvery` or keep the default cycle, and explain the cycle in the surrounding text.

## Motion

- The amount rises above the customer, the card details travel to the gateway, and the request crosses the card
  network to the issuing bank.
- The issuer's decision shows as a green Approved or red Declined badge, and the response returns on the lower lane.
- An approved payment settles along the dashed line to the merchant account, and the balance readout increases.
- Reduced motion and Off show the approved path as a still frame with the Approved and Paid badges. The play button
  is hidden.

| Change | Full | Reduced | Off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amount and request travel | Animated packets on each route, with the amount badge above the customer | Still frame of the approved path | Still frame of the approved path |
| Gateway and issuer state | "Tokenized" badge pops in; the issuer's ring turns on while it checks | Shown in the final state | Shown in the final state |
| Decision | Badge pops in, response travels back on the lower lane | Approved badge and success route | Approved badge and success route |
| Settlement and balance | Dashed line runs to the merchant; the readout moves to the new balance | Readout shows the opening balance plus the amount | Readout shows the opening balance plus the amount |
| Play button | Visible; toggles playback | Hidden | Hidden |

## Related

- `DataFlow` for the pipeline that stores events after a payment is completed.
- `MultiRegionFailover` for keeping the payment service available when a region fails.
- `Stepper` for a fixed sequence of steps that the user moves through.

| Component | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `MoneyInput` | The customer types an amount that must be parsed and formatted |
| `Alert` | You state that a payment failed, or that a service is down, in text |
| `Timeline` | You show the events of one real transaction in order, with their times |
| `DataGrid` | You list past payments with amounts, dates and decline codes |
| `BarChart` / `LineChart` | You plot revenue, volume or decline rates over time |
| `Stepper` | The user moves through the steps of a checkout |
| `MultiRegionFailover` | The story is about a region failing while the service stays available |

# Multi-region failover

> A global load balancer shifts traffic to a standby region and promotes its database when the primary region goes down.

- Package: `TKCode.Arc`, `dotnet add package TKCode.Arc --version 0.3.2-preview.1`
- XAML namespace: `xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"`
- Live page: https://docs.tkcode.si/components/multi-region-failover

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.MultiRegionFailoverAutomaticFailoverDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="12">
        <arc:MultiRegionFailover x:Name="Failover" />
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="0.5×" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnHalfSpeedClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="1×" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnNormalSpeedClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="2×" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnDoubleSpeedClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Start over" Variant="Ghost" Size="Small" Click="OnRestartClick" />
        </WrapPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class MultiRegionFailoverAutomaticFailoverDemo : UserControl
{
    public MultiRegionFailoverAutomaticFailoverDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnHalfSpeedClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.Speed = 0.5;
    }

    private void OnNormalSpeedClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.Speed = 1;
    }

    private void OnDoubleSpeedClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.Speed = 2;
    }

    private void OnRestartClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.Restart();
    }
}
```

## When to use

`MultiRegionFailover` shows how a service stays available when one of its regions fails. It draws the global traffic
path, each region with its application and database, and the replication links between the databases, then plays the
failure, the traffic shift, the database promotion and the recovery. It belongs on architecture and reliability pages,
in runbooks and in training material, where the reader needs to know which region serves traffic and which database
accepts writes at any moment.

- **Reliability page for a payment or billing API**: a page that explains why checkout keeps working when
  `us-east-1` is down. The primary region serves traffic, `eu-west-1` holds a replica that is promoted, and the caption
  describes what happens to in-flight requests.
- **Runbook rehearsal before a game day**: a team walks through a failover of an order database with the manual
  controls, using the same state machine as the diagram, before it runs the real procedure in production.
- **Architecture review of a multi-region deployment**: a design document that compares a two-region active-passive
  layout with a three-region layout, using the `Regions` property to show each variant.
- **Onboarding for on-call engineers**: a short explanation of what "promoted" and "replica" mean for the team's own
  database, placed next to the runbook steps they will follow.
- **Customer documentation for a data residency feature**: an explanation of where data is replicated and which region
  takes over, with the region names the customer's contract uses.

## When not to use

- **A notice that a real service is down**: use `Alert` with the actual status text and the time of the incident. The
  diagram plays a fixed story and must never stand in for the real state of production.
- **A single region or a single server**: the story needs two or three regions to make sense. Use `Card` with plain
  text, or a `Timeline` of the incident, when only one location is involved.
- **Real uptime, latency or error rates**: use `LineChart` or `Gauge` with the measured values. The illustration shows
  the shape of a failover, not how long your failovers took.
- **A live health view of every region**: use `DataGrid` or a list of `Badge` values with the health check results.
  Ten regions or a dozen health checks do not fit the three-region frame.
- **A procedure people follow step by step**: use `Stepper` for the runbook steps and link the diagram beside it. The
  illustration loops on its own and cannot wait for the operator to confirm a step.

## Usage

By default the story plays by itself: a region fails its health checks, traffic and the primary database move to a
standby region, the failed region recovers as a replica, and traffic returns to the planned region. The control needs
no data and no code to run.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc">
    <arc:MultiRegionFailover />
</UserControl>
```

`MultiRegionFailover` derives from `Illustration`, which derives from Avalonia's `TemplatedControl`. It takes focus,
has a `Label` for assistive technology, and uses the same frame, playback button and caption as the other system
illustrations. The control keeps a small state machine for each region: healthy, degraded, down or recovering. Every
visible change in the diagram is a transition of that state machine, so the diagram never shows a state the code
cannot reach.

### Anatomy

1. **Users** (`Labels.Users`, `Labels.UsersDetail`): the source of traffic at the top left, 150 by 52 scene units.
2. **Global balancer** (`Labels.Balancer`, `Labels.BalancerDetail`): a wider card at the top centre, 170 by 52 units,
   with the traffic path from the users. Beside it, a readout shows the region that receives traffic
   (`Labels.ServedBy`) and, during a switch, the failover time (`Labels.FailoverTime`).
3. **Region frames**: two or three groups across the lower part of the scene, named by the region. Each frame has a
   health dot, a title and a status word (`Labels.Healthy`, `Labels.Degraded`, `Labels.Down` or `Labels.Recovering`)
   drawn above the connections, so the lines never cross the text.
4. **Application** (`Labels.App`, `Labels.AppDetail`): the service in each region, with the traffic line from the
   balancer.
5. **Database** (`Labels.Database`, and a subtitle that reads `Labels.Primary`, `Labels.Replica`,
   `Labels.Unavailable` or "replica · catching up"): the data store in each region, with a link from the application.
6. **Replication links**: dashed lines between neighbouring databases in the order of the `Regions` list. Changes
   travel along them as green packets.
7. **Badges**: a "Failing over" badge on the balancer during a switch, and a "Promoted" badge on the database that
   became primary. The badge text comes from `Labels.FailingOver`, `Labels.Promoted` and `Labels.Primary`.
8. **Caption line** (`IsCaptionVisible`) and **play button** (`IsPlaybackButtonVisible`): the same controls as the
   other illustrations. The button is hidden in the still poster.

The scene is 844 by 356 units and scales to the width the control is given. The frame keeps 20 px of padding on the
sides and top and 14 px at the bottom, and the nodes use the 12 px corner radius of the token.

Health is shown in three tones: a degraded region turns warning, a down region turns danger and its packets are
dropped, and a recovered region returns to success.

### Regions

`Regions` takes two or three region names. A list with fewer than two names falls back to the default regions
(`us-east-1`, `eu-west-1` and `ap-southeast-1`), and a list with more than three uses the first three. The region
frames share the scene width evenly, so two regions give wider frames than three.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:generic="using:System.Collections.Generic"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.MultiRegionFailoverTwoRegionsDemo">
    <arc:MultiRegionFailover>
        <arc:MultiRegionFailover.Regions>
            <generic:List x:TypeArguments="x:String">
                <x:String>primary-fra</x:String>
                <x:String>standby-ams</x:String>
            </generic:List>
        </arc:MultiRegionFailover.Regions>
    </arc:MultiRegionFailover>
</UserControl>
```

The first region in the list starts as the primary, and the second is the standby. With two regions, every failure of
the primary moves traffic and the primary to the other region, and the failover is the only path the story can take.
With three regions, the failover goes to the next healthy region in the list, wrapping around at the end, so the order
of the list is the order of preference. Put the region that should take over first directly after the primary.

### Driving the failure yourself

Set `IsAutomatic` to `False` to stop the scripted story, and call `FailRegion` and `RecoverRegion` with the index of the
region. Each call runs the same state machine as the automatic story, so the diagram and the readouts behave the same way.

- `FailRegion(index)` takes a region down. It is ignored when the index is out of range or the region is already
  degraded or down.
- `RecoverRegion(index)` brings a region back. It is ignored when the index is out of range or the region is already
  healthy or recovering.
- `PrimaryRegion` is the index of the region whose database is primary, and `TrafficRegion` is the index of the region
  that receives traffic. Both are read-only.
- `PrimaryRegionChanged` is raised with the index of the new primary after a promotion. It is not raised when a
  region that holds no primary role fails.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.MultiRegionFailoverDriveItYourselfDemo">
    <StackPanel Spacing="12">
        <arc:MultiRegionFailover x:Name="Failover"
                                 IsAutomatic="False"
                                 PrimaryRegionChanged="OnPrimaryRegionChanged" />
        <WrapPanel HorizontalAlignment="Center" ItemSpacing="12" LineSpacing="12">
            <arc:Button Content="Fail us-east-1" Variant="Danger" Size="Small" Click="OnFailEastClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Recover us-east-1" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnRecoverEastClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Fail eu-west-1" Variant="Danger" Size="Small" Click="OnFailWestClick" />
            <arc:Button Content="Recover eu-west-1" Variant="Secondary" Size="Small" Click="OnRecoverWestClick" />
            <TextBlock x:Name="Primary"
                       Text="Primary: us-east-1"
                       FontSize="13"
                       TextWrapping="Wrap"
                       VerticalAlignment="Center"
                       Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextMuted}" />
        </WrapPanel>
    </StackPanel>
</UserControl>
```

```cs
using Avalonia.Controls;
using Avalonia.Interactivity;

namespace TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos;

public partial class MultiRegionFailoverDriveItYourselfDemo : UserControl
{
    public MultiRegionFailoverDriveItYourselfDemo()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
    }

    private void OnPrimaryRegionChanged(object? sender, int index)
    {
        Primary.Text = $"Primary: {MultiRegionFailover.DefaultRegions[index]}";
    }

    private void OnFailEastClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.FailRegion(0);
    }

    private void OnRecoverEastClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.RecoverRegion(0);
    }

    private void OnFailWestClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.FailRegion(1);
    }

    private void OnRecoverWestClick(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e)
    {
        Failover.RecoverRegion(1);
    }
}
```

```csharp
var failover = new MultiRegionFailover { IsAutomatic = false };
var regionNames = new[] { "us-east-1", "eu-west-1", "ap-southeast-1" };

failover.PrimaryRegionChanged += (_, index) =>
    primaryLabel.Text = $"Primary: {regionNames[index]}";

failButton.Click += (_, _) => failover.FailRegion(0);
recoverButton.Click += (_, _) => failover.RecoverRegion(0);
```

The failure is a sequence, not a single change. A failed region shows a degraded state for 0.8 seconds, then a down
state. If it held traffic or the primary, the load balancer switches to the next healthy region 0.5 seconds later, and
if it held the primary database, the next healthy region's database is promoted 0.7 seconds after that. The failover
time readout counts from the failure to the traffic switch. The timings are scene time, so a paused illustration
finishes the sequence when it plays again.

Use the controls to rehearse a failure. Name them after the action and the region, such as "Fail us-east-1" and
"Recover us-east-1", so each button is clear to a screen reader and to the operator reading the page.

### Labels

`Labels` takes a `MultiRegionFailoverLabels` object with every visible word of the diagram: the node names and details,
the health states, the badges and the step captions. Set only the properties you need, and keep the wording of the
step captions consistent with the runbook, because the caption is the only explanation a reader sees while the story
runs.

```csharp
failover.Labels = new MultiRegionFailoverLabels
{
    Balancer = "Global LB",
    FailingOver = "Switching",
    Promoted = "Now primary"
};
```

### Playback

`IsPlaying`, `Speed` and `Restart()` control the story in the same way as on the other illustrations. `Speed` takes
values from 0.25 to 4. The automatic story has six steps, and `StepChanged` reports each one:

| Step | Caption | When it happens (automatic story) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Traffic is served from the planned region; data replicates to the standby regions | Start |
| 1 | A region fails its health checks | At 3.0 s, when the region fails |
| 2 | The load balancer shifts traffic to the next healthy region | About 1.3 s after the failure |
| 3 | The standby database is promoted to primary | About 2.0 s after the failure |
| 4 | The failed region recovers and catches up as a replica | At 8.6 s, when it recovers |
| 5 | A planned failback to the original region | At 11.8 s; the loop is 14.4 s long |

The story ends on a planned failback, which moves traffic and the primary back to the first region. The manual
controls do not fail back on their own; see the common questions below.

```xml
<arc:MultiRegionFailover Speed="2" />
```

### Reduced motion

Under reduced motion (or Off) the illustration is a still frame of the healthy deployment. Traffic is served from the
first region, the standby replication links are drawn dashed, and the caption summarizes the deployment. The play
button is hidden. Use the still frame on pages where the reader needs the topology but not the sequence.

```xml
<UserControl xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
             xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
             xmlns:arc="https://github.com/AIDotNet/TKCode.Arc"
             x:Class="TKCode.Arc.Gallery.Demos.MultiRegionFailoverReducedMotionDemo">
    <arc:MultiRegionFailover arc:ArcMotion.Level="Reduced" />
</UserControl>
```

### Driving it from code

The control is a demonstration of a state machine, not a reader of your infrastructure. Use it to show a failover
that has already happened, or one you want to rehearse, and keep the real state in your monitoring system. A reasonable
pattern is to keep the illustration on a page that explains the design and to drive it from the operator's own
controls, as in the sample above. Do not connect a health check feed directly to `FailRegion`: the control would then
animate a failure that the feed reports, without any of the checks, timeouts and approvals of a real failover.

### Example: payments platform reliability page

A reliability page for a billing service. The regions are the ones the service actually runs in, the balancer is
named with the short form the infrastructure team uses, and the database and application labels describe the roles in the
architecture. The caption explains what the reader sees while the story plays, so the page does not depend on the
animation alone.

![A three-region deployment with a global load balancer and a primary database in us-east-1](https://docs.tkcode.si/shots/Docs/Illustrations/MultiRegionFailover/images/PaymentsRegions.webp)

```xml
<StackPanel Width="760" Spacing="16">
    <TextBlock Text="How billing stays available"
               FontSize="16"
               FontWeight="SemiBold"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource Foreground}" />
    <TextBlock Text="Requests are served from the primary region. When it fails, traffic and the primary database move to the next healthy region."
               TextWrapping="Wrap"
               Foreground="{arc:ArcDesignTokenResource TextSecondary}" />
    <arc:MultiRegionFailover Label="Billing service failover across three regions">
        <arc:MultiRegionFailover.Labels>
            <arc:MultiRegionFailoverLabels Users="Customers"
                                           UsersDetail="worldwide"
                                           Balancer="Global LB"
                                           BalancerDetail="health checks"
                                           App="Billing API"
                                           AppDetail="3 instances"
                                           Database="Ledger DB"
                                           FailingOver="Failing over" />
        </arc:MultiRegionFailover.Labels>
    </arc:MultiRegionFailover>
</StackPanel>
```

The labels are short on purpose: the balancer card is narrower than the region cards, and a longer title is cut off
with an ellipsis. Check the screenshot after you change a label.

### Content guidelines

Name the regions as the infrastructure names them, and name the database roles with the words the team uses in its
runbook (primary, replica). Write the balancer as the component's job ("Global load balancer", "Traffic manager"),
not as a product name, unless the page is about that product. Keep the captions in the present tense, and describe the
state, not the team's response ("Traffic is served from eu-west-1", not "We moved traffic").

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| Highly available across all regions | Traffic is served from eu-west-1 while us-east-1 is down |
| Region 1 | us-east-1 |
| Master DB | Primary database |
| Slave | Replica |
| Failover complete | Traffic is served from eu-west-1 |
| The system heals itself | The failed region recovers and catches up as a replica |

Do not promise a failover time in a label. The failover readout is the time the diagram took, and a customer-facing
claim must come from your own measurements, stated next to the diagram.

### Best practices

**Do**

- Show the same regions as your production deployment. A readout that names regions the service does not run in
  teaches the wrong topology, and a reader cannot tell the difference.
- Keep the failover order in the `Regions` list in the order of preference, and say so on the page, because the next
  healthy region in the list receives the traffic.
- Use `IsAutomatic="False"` with real buttons on runbook pages, so the operator decides when each step happens.
- Provide the state in text beside the diagram. Assistive technology does not read the caption changes, so the page
  must state the current situation in words.

**Avoid**

- Using the diagram as the status of a real service. A story that loops would show a failure that may not exist. Use
  `Alert` for real status.
- Labelling the readouts with measured values you have not measured. The failover time is scene time, not a
  benchmark.
- Leaving the automatic story on a page that explains a specific incident. The story loops and implies the incident is
  still happening.
- Connecting a live health feed to `FailRegion` or `RecoverRegion`. Those calls animate the state machine and do not
  move any real traffic, so the diagram can disagree with production.

### Common questions

**How do I stop the automatic story and drive the failure myself?** Set `IsAutomatic` to `False`. The scripted failure,
recovery and failback stop, and the state changes only when you call `FailRegion` or `RecoverRegion`. Changing
`IsAutomatic` rebuilds the diagram, so set it before the page shows the control.

**Why is the failover time not the time from my monitoring alarm?** The readout is the scene time between the call to
`FailRegion` and the traffic switch. It describes the diagram's sequence, which uses fixed delays (0.8 and 0.5 seconds),
and it is not a measurement of your system.

**Does recovery move traffic back?** No. `RecoverRegion` brings the region back as a replica and catches it up, but
traffic and the primary role stay where the failover put them. Only the automatic story performs a planned failback.
Traffic stays on the promoted region until that region fails.

**What happens when no other region is healthy?** The failed region keeps traffic and the primary. The failover
does not start, so `TrafficRegion` and `PrimaryRegion` do not change and `PrimaryRegionChanged` is not raised.

**Which regions does the replication follow?** Replication runs between neighbouring databases in the order of the
`Regions` list, one hop at a time. A standby beyond a region that is down receives nothing until that region
recovers, and a recovered region receives a short burst of catch-up changes from the primary.

## API reference

### MultiRegionFailover

An animated multi-region deployment: a global load balancer sends users to the primary region while its database replicates to standby regions. When a region fails its health checks traffic shifts to the next healthy region and, if it held the primary database, a replica is promoted; a recovered region catches up as a replica.

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Regions` | `IReadOnlyList<string>?` | `null` | The regions (2 or 3 names); defaults to us-east-1, eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1. |
| `IsAutomatic` | `bool` | `true` | Plays the failure and recovery story by itself (default); false waits for `FailRegion`. |
| `Labels` | `MultiRegionFailoverLabels` | – | Node titles, badges and caption text of the diagram; set it to rename or translate the scene. |
| `IsPlaying` | `bool` | `true` | Whether the illustration plays (two way). Paused, it holds the current frame. |
| `Speed` | `double` | `1` | Playback speed (0.25–4). |
| `Label` | `string?` | `"Multi-region failover illustration"` | The accessible name of the illustration. |
| `IsCaptionVisible` | `bool` | `true` | Shows the caption line under the diagram. |
| `IsPlaybackButtonVisible` | `bool` | `true` | Shows the play / pause button. |
| `Caption` | `string` | – | *Read-only.* What the current step shows (also the accessible help text). |
| `Step` | `int` | – | *Read-only.* The current step (0-based); see `StepCount`. |

| Event | Arguments | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `PrimaryRegionChanged` | `int` | Raised when another region's database becomes the primary. |
| `StepChanged` | `IllustrationStepChangedEventArgs` | Raised when the story moves to another step. |

Pseudo-classes: `:playing`, `:poster`

Derives from `TemplatedControl`: every member of `TemplatedControl` works as well.

### MultiRegionFailoverLabels

Every visible word of a `MultiRegionFailover` (override for another language or domain).

Failover events use the standard `EventHandler<int>` with the index of the new primary as the argument.

## Accessibility

- `Label` is the accessible name of the illustration. Name the deployment in it, for example "Billing service failover
  across three regions".
- The illustration takes focus and shows a 2px focus ring around the frame when it is focused.
- The current caption is exposed as the help text, so a screen reader hears what the step means when the control has
  focus.
- Caption changes are not announced, because the story loops and would repeat the same message without end.
- The region names, health states and badges are the text of the diagram. Keep them meaningful on their own, because
  a reader who cannot see the animation still gets the topology from the labels.
- The manual controls must be real buttons with their own names, such as "Fail us-east-1". A button labelled only
  "Fail" does not say which region it affects.
- Under reduced motion the still frame gives the healthy topology with its summary caption, so the state is clear
  without any movement.

### Keyboard

The illustration takes focus with Tab. Once it has focus, these keys control the automatic story:

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` | Move focus to or from the illustration |
| `Space` or `Enter` | Play or pause the story |
| `R` | Start the story over from its healthy state |

The keyboard does not fail or recover a region. Provide buttons for that, and give them keyboard access in the same
way as the rest of the page.

## Motion

- The failing region turns amber, then red, and the packets in transit to it are dropped.
- The load balancer switches traffic to a healthy region with a "Failing over" badge, and the readout shows the time
  the switch took.
- The standby database is promoted with a "Promoted" badge, and replication runs from the new primary.
- Recovery shows the region catching up as a replica, followed by the planned failback in the automatic story.

| Change | Full | Reduced | Off |
|---|---|---|---|
| A region fails | Frame turns warning, then danger; its packets fade out and its links dim | Shown in the steady state, which is healthy | Shown in the steady state |
| Traffic moves to another region | Traffic lines crossfade over 0.4 s; the failover badge shows during the switch | Not shown | Not shown |
| The database is promoted | "Promoted" badge pops in; the replication links run from the new primary | Not shown | Not shown |
| A region recovers | Frame returns to success after the catch-up burst | Not shown | Not shown |
| Play button | Visible; toggles playback | Hidden | Hidden |

## Related

- `PaymentFlow` for a single request that depends on the payment service being available.
- `DataFlow` for a pipeline that stores events in one warehouse.
- `Alert` for stating the status of a real service in text.

| Component | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `Alert` | You state the status of a real service or incident in text |
| `Stepper` | The runbook steps are a sequence the operator moves through |
| `Timeline` | You show what happened during a real incident, in order and with times |
| `LineChart` / `Gauge` | You plot measured uptime, latency or error rates |
| `DataGrid` | You list the health of every region or every check in a table |
| `PaymentFlow` | The story is one payment request that depends on the service |
| `DataFlow` | The story is events moving from sources to a warehouse |
